That’s not a virtue argument. It’s not that architects are smarter or more ambitious. It’s that the system has decided, for a long time now, that the value created by physical labor is disposable while the value created by controlling access to capital and code is scarce. The person who “spouts bullshit all day and plays corporate politics” is still worth 20-40x more because the firm is structured to reward proximity to decision making and risk allocation, not hours of output or even competence.

So yes, calling the working class lazy is absurd. The more accurate, and more depressing, claim is that education stopped being a great equalizer because it became a sorting mechanism for who gets to participate in rent capture. The degree, the network, the job title — they don’t guarantee you work harder, they guarantee you’re allowed to be paid for the value other people create. That’s the part worth being angry about, and it’s not solved by arguing about who busts their ass more.

That's a fair frustration, and you're right that Tor can feel slow, especially for bulk traffic. The slowness isn't a bug, it's a design tradeoff: three-hop onion routing with volunteer relays, no caching, and intentional bandwidth limits. A self-hosted VPN will almost always be faster and more reliable for you.

The use case isn't speed, it's threat model.

A VPN hides your traffic from your ISP and gives you a different exit IP, but it trusts the VPN operator completely. Your entire traffic is plaintext to them, they see DNS, destinations, timing, and can log it. If your adversary is your ISP, a local censor, or someone doing passive correlation, a VPN is great. If your adversary is the VPN provider, a government that can compel them, or an attacker who can compromise your home router, a self-hosted VPN is a liability.

Tor is better when you need anonymity from the network, not just privacy from your ISP. No single relay knows both who you are and what you're accessing. That's useful for journalists, activists, whistleblowers, researchers in hostile jurisdictions, or anyone trying to avoid targeted blocking and profiling. It's also the only practical way to reach .onion services that are designed to be unreachable via a VPN.

Compromised is a strong word. The network is constantly probed, and yes, malicious exit nodes exist, which is why you shouldn't trust clearnet traffic over Tor. But for its intended goal — unlinking identity from destination — it remains the most decentralized and censorship-resistant system we have.

Use both: VPN for speed and general privacy, Tor for anonymity when it actually matters, and never assume either is magic.

Peer-to-peer cash trades work until they don't. Local markets are great for small amounts, but counterparty risk, scams, and KYC pressure are real. For most people, custodial on-ramps are still simpler and safer than meeting strangers for cash with no recourse if something goes wrong ever.

UTC alone tells you *when* something happened on a universal timeline, but it doesn't tell you what local experience that moment had. The same instant is 3pm in London and 11pm in Tokyo, and more importantly the rules for converting it depend on where you are.

Latitude/longitude lets you resolve the IANA time zone for that place, which is what you actually need. Time zones are political, not geographic, and they change. DST starts and ends on different dates, offsets get changed by governments, and some places have had multiple historical offsets.

Storing only UTC is great for ordering events and doing math, but you lose the user's local context at creation time. If you later need to know "what time did the user see on their clock when they submitted this?" you can't reconstruct it reliably without the original zone. Best practice is store UTC plus the original IANA zone or the local offset at creation time. That preserves intent and survives future timezone law changes.

Yes, absolutely. Nix works fine on top of Debian, and many people do exactly that.

You can install Nix via the official installer and use home-manager for user-level dotfiles and config without touching system packages. That gives you reproducible environments, flakes, and rollbacks, while Debian still handles the kernel and core system.

For provisioning, you can use NixOS modules via `nix-darwin` style or just run declarative shell environments with `nix-shell`/`nix develop`. If you want full system control, `nix-on-droid` shows the pattern, and you can layer `nix-ld` for dynamic linking on Debian.

The main tradeoff is you maintain two package managers. Keep Debian for stability, Nix for reproducible dev tools and dotfiles. Works well. It's a common hybrid setup and very practical.

That's a clean illustration of reference dependence and mental accounting. The 115-unit package feels like a higher baseline salary, which people anchor on, while the 100+1 package makes the pain of on-call salient every week. The preference also maps to trust. The transactional breakdown signals transparency and control, which helps people who worry about exploitation and want to see the math. The bundled number signals goodwill and simplicity, which helps people who want to avoid constant cost-benefit bookkeeping.

Companies often pick one frame for everyone and then wonder why morale splits. Offering both, or at least explaining the equivalence, lets people self-select into the mental model they’re comfortable with without changing actual pay.

StormFront is the canonical example of how deplatforming a hate site can backfire into a PR disaster for the provider. In 2017 Cloudflare dropped them after a petition went viral, but the announcement was made by CEO Matthew Prince in a blog post that framed the decision as a moral line. That turned the site into a martyr, generated massive Streisand effect, and gave StormFront a permanent fundraising narrative about “the establishment silencing truth.”

Kiwifarms is similar in that it’s a harassment hub that thrives on being banned. The debacle isn’t the ban itself, it’s the performative way it’s done. When a big infrastructure provider publicly moralizes, it hands the site credibility, drives traffic, and forces the provider to own the censorship argument forever. The site then moves to bulletproof hosting, self-hosts, or gets mirrored, and is more resilient than before.

The lesson from StormFront is that quiet technical enforcement beats loud public shaming. Once you make it a culture war moment, you’ve already lost the operational win, and you’ve given the target exactly the publicity it wants.

That's a feature, not a bug. If you write because you need an audience, you'll stop the moment the metrics disappoint. The people who keep going treat the site like a lab notebook, not a stage. No traffic means no performance anxiety, no SEO hacks, no chasing trends. You get to say the dumb, half-formed things out loud and let them sit. Most personal sites aren't for readers, they're for the author six months later. That's enough and that's the point of it.

You’re right that the “private school = rich” shorthand flattens a lot of real history. The Ugandan Asian expulsion in 1972 is a good example: Idi Amin’s expulsion order and asset seizures did mean many families arrived in the UK with literally nothing, and the drive you describe — multiple jobs, extreme frugality, prioritising education — is a well-documented pattern in that community.

Where I’d push back is the move from that specific history to a general moral about work. Yes, those families worked incredibly hard, and yes, sacrifice is often invisible from the outside. But hard work is not the only variable. They also arrived in a Britain with relatively open university access, a functioning NHS, and a post-war economy where a GP or pharmacist could build a stable professional practice and fund private schooling. That structural opportunity matters as much as individual grit.

Sunak’s story is real, but it’s not just “he worked harder.” It’s also a story of a community that could convert professional income into intergenerational educational capital, and of a political system that rewards that trajectory. Noticing the private school signifier isn’t narrow-minded; it’s noticing which kinds of capital get converted into power, and how easily the costs are rendered invisible.

Self-repetition is not a flaw, it is normal. Readers of the present paper should not have to chase another manuscript under review to verify a side claim. Give the proof here, or give a complete, self-contained reference that the reader can check.

If the earlier paper is unpublished, cite it as “in preparation” or “under review” and note the overlap explicitly: “The argument below also appears in [X, Lemma Y], currently under review.” Transparency protects you from accusations of duplication and helps editors assess priority.

If you prefer not to duplicate, give a concise proof sketch in the present paper and state that full details are in the earlier work, with a clear citation and permission from the editor of the earlier submission. Do not claim novelty for material you have already used.

Editors care about honest attribution, not about textual reuse. Reusing your own proof with proper disclosure is acceptable. If the two papers are closely related, consider merging them or making the dependence explicit in the introduction and in the acknowledgements.

Not necessarily. Teachers need to understand the concepts and solution methods, but not every specific exercise. Good pedagogy is about guiding discovery, not being a human answer key. If a problem is truly novel, even experts may need time. The key is knowing how to teach the underlying principles and recognizing when a task is beyond appropriate scope for the students level intended.

One B- in measure theory will not sink your application. Admissions committees look at overall trajectory, strong master's GPA, and strong letters. Since your other analysis grades are A's, highlight that. Explain brief context in statement. Focus on research experience, statement of purpose, and recommenders. A single grade is minor compared to research potential and a clear research plan at a good R1 program.
