No, an unsolicited reference letter is not inherently a black mark, and in most cases it will not hurt you. Search committees are used to receiving extra material, and a good letter from a known scholar can only help, especially in a small field like mathematics where referees may know each other.

The concern about looking disorganised is understandable but unlikely to be an issue. Committees do not expect you to police who writes on your behalf, and omitting a name from your list is normal; you listed the references you asked, not an exhaustive list of everyone who might write. If the letter is positive, the committee will simply treat it as additional support.

The only risk would be if the unsolicited letter were negative or contradictory, or if it raised questions about your judgment. A good letter is an asset. You can, if you wish, inform the committee chair that you were unaware of the letter, but it is not required.

Yes, you can keep it as a pre-print and not attend, but it is not the same as a conference publication.

For a CS PhD admissions committee, a paper in the proceedings of a recognized conference, even a top-80 venue, signals peer review, vetting, and commitment to the community. A pre-print signals interesting ideas but no external validation. As an undergrad, one peer-reviewed conference paper carries significantly more weight than an arXiv-only pre-print, especially when you are competing with applicants who have formal publications.

You also need to check the conference policy. Many conferences require registration for at least one author for the paper to appear in the proceedings. If you do not register and pay, your paper may be withdrawn and will not be published. That withdrawal is worse than a pre-print, because it looks like you could not follow through.

If you do register and the paper is published, you can still post the pre-print version on arXiv with a note that a revised version appears in the conference proceedings. That is normal. Do not post the camera-ready version if the conference requires copyright transfer.

Since you plan to extend the work for a journal, be careful about prior publication and self-plagiarism. Most journals allow substantial extension of a conference paper, but you must cite it and ensure the overlap is limited to the original results. Keeping the conference version in the proceedings helps establish priority.

In short: attend virtually if possible, register if you can afford it, publish in the proceedings, and post a pre-print for visibility. The formal publication will help your PhD application far more than a pre-print alone.

The LNCS proceedings listing is sufficient proof of publication. For a PhD admissions panel in the US, what matters is that the paper is peer-reviewed and archived in a citable, verifiable venue.

The certificate of attendance is proof of presentation, not proof of authorship. Authorship is established by the bibliographic record: title, authors, venue name, year, volume, pages, DOI/ISBN, and the paper being indexed in LNCS, SpringerLink, DBLP, Scopus, Web of Science, etc.

List the paper on your CV with full citation and provide a link to the SpringerLink page or DBLP entry. If you did not attend, note that clearly; non-attendance does not invalidate publication. If asked, you can provide the acceptance email and the proceedings PDF.

Only request a certificate if the conference explicitly requires physical presence for inclusion in proceedings. Most LNCS conferences include all accepted papers regardless of registration.

Quitting a PhD for mental health is not a career death sentence, especially early. Admissions committees care more about trajectory than perfection, and a first-term withdrawal leaves little academic record to explain.

Be honest with yourself first: prioritize treatment and stability. A degree is not worth your life. If you leave now, document your progress, request a neutral completion letter, and keep your recommenders informed.

Later reapplication is absolutely possible. Many successful researchers took breaks, switched fields, or started over. Industry research roles like those at OpenAI value skills, publications, and internships more than a linear PhD path.

Give yourself recovery time before deciding. You can return to research when you are healthier, and that version of you will be a stronger candidate. Your health must come first. Please stay safe.

Yes. Use the grant number on the EU Funding & Tenders Portal or CORDIS. The project page lists partners, work packages and often the individual PhD topics. The official Grant Agreement and published recruitment documents usually detail each position. Contact the coordinator for the specific project descriptions and full research plans if needed.

A PhD is not a credential for "official" knowledge, it is training to produce original research under supervision. If you are not pursuing an academic career in history, a second doctorate is excessive and will not certify what you already know.

Better ways to formalize expertise depend on your goal. For public recognition, publish: articles in peer-reviewed journals, a monograph with a university press, or well-sourced essays in reputable magazines. For academic recognition, present at conferences, join scholarly societies, and seek peer review.

If you want formal study without a doctorate, consider a taught MA in history, certificates in public history, or auditing courses. These signal commitment and give you credentials without the multi-year research commitment of a PhD.

Ultimately, expertise is demonstrated by what you produce and who engages with it, not by collecting degrees.

Clamp-on cages work fine on most mountain bikes, even with wide down tubes. Look for a universal mount with adjustable straps, like the Topeak Modula or Blackburn Outpost, which fit 28-45mm tubes. 

If your frame is carbon, avoid clamps and use a seatpost or stem mount instead. A seatpost-mounted cage keeps the bottle accessible and clears suspension.

Measure your tube diameter first. Most clamps fit up to 40mm; for wider tubes get an adapter or a strap-on cage. They’re cheap, tool-free, and removable without drilling for daily trail use

The stem cap and top bolt you are missing is the headset pre-load cap. It is a standard part and very easy to source, but the problem in your update is not just the cap.

The bolt is spinning because there is nothing for it to pull against inside the steerer tube. On a threadless fork the cap pushes the stem down onto the headset bearings via a star nut or a compression expander that sits inside the steerer. Your photos show the steerer is empty, the star nut is missing and has probably been lost with the cap.

You need a new star nut for a 1 1/8" steerer, or if the steerer is carbon an external compression plug, plus a new top cap and bolt. A star nut is about £5-10 and the cap and bolt kit is similar. Halfords will have both and can fit it in minutes.

Fitting is simple if you have a star nut setter. The nut is tapped into the top of the steerer about 15-20mm down, then the fork is inserted, stem fitted, cap bolted down to remove play from the headset without overtightening the stem bolts. Do not use the top bolt to clamp the stem.

If you are unsure, take the bike to Halfords. They can check the steerer is not damaged and install the correct nut and cap, and make sure the headset is correctly pre-loaded. It is a cheap, quick job and avoids damaging the steerer.

Your squeak is likely bearing preload, not size. Square-taper cartridge BBs should be tightened to ~35-50 Nm on the drive side, then back off until smooth. The 118mm to 115mm change won't fix binding; it just moves chainline. With an eccentric shell for belt tension you can keep chainline correct, but the binding suggests over-tightening or a cheap unit with poor tolerances.

A Shimano UN55 is excellent for the price and will last far longer than a no-name. Fit the same 118mm unless you want a slightly narrower Q-factor.

Small glass cuts in Gatorskin tread don’t need filling. The casing is intact and the rubber is thick, so sealant stays inside. Just remove shards, inspect for deeper cuts, and ride. If a cut is deep enough to expose cords, replace the tire. Otherwise cleaning and monitoring is sufficient for routine use and regular pressure checks

The RD-M9000 doesn’t have a traditional barrel adjuster on the derailleur body like older Shimano road derailleurs. On 11 speed XTR Shadow Plus the cable tension adjustment is moved up to the shifter and / or an inline adjuster.

The RD-M9000 uses Shimano’s Shadow design with the cable entering the derailleur from below and clamping on the inner plate. There is no threaded barrel on the derailleur itself. The only adjustments on the derailleur are:

* H and L limit screws for total travel
* B-tension screw for upper pulley to cassette clearance
* The pulley cage angle / clutch

Cable tension is set at the shifter end. On the XTR M9000 I-Spec II shifter the right hand shifter has a small knurled barrel adjuster on the underside of the shifter body where the cable exits. Turn it clockwise to increase tension, moving the derailleur outwards toward larger cogs, counter-clockwise to decrease tension.

If you are running a non-I-Spec setup or a remote dropper, you will normally have an inline barrel adjuster on the housing run between shifter and derailleur. That is the equivalent you are used to. Shimano sells SM-CB90 and similar inline adjusters for exactly this purpose.

If you have no inline adjuster, the only way to trim is at the shifter. Some riders add a Jagwire or Shimano inline adjuster to the rear cable for convenience. Once installed, use it to dial out rub in the middle of the cassette after you have set limit screws, B-tension and cable clamp tension with the derailleur in the smallest cog.

Do not try to adjust tension by loosening the cable anchor bolt on the derailleur and re-clamping; that is for initial installation only and will throw off your indexing.

Removing bosses is irreversible and costly for little gain. A good framebuilder can do it cleanly, but you’ll lose resale value and the option to run cantilevers or discs later. Since your model was made with calipers, just fit a caliper fork and rear bridge or use a long-reach caliper on the existing bosses. Respraying is the perfect time to add cable stops if needed, but keep the frame intact.

Store the unmounted tires in a sealed plastic bin with tight lid. For the mounted bike, keep it elevated on a wall mount or high rack cats can’t reach. Apply bitter apple spray to sidewalls and cover tires with loose-fitting old socks when parked. Cats dislike texture and taste, and elevation removes easy access for good measure.

Bicycle tires puncture more often because they are much more vulnerable, not because roads are worse. A car tire is 4–6 times wider and holds 30–35 psi, with a large air volume and a thick steel-belted rubber carcass that can roll over a nail without letting it reach the tube. The contact patch is big, so pressure on the road is low.

A bicycle tire is narrow, runs at 60–120 psi, and has a thin carcass and a small, flexible tube. The high pressure means a tiny sharp object can easily penetrate the tread, and the small volume means a pinhole causes rapid deflation. You also ride much closer to the road surface, pick debris from the gutter, and the bike is lighter so it does not push hazards aside. Fewer tires, more miles per tire, and you notice every flat makes the rate look dramatic.

Yes, Shimano road calipers and rotors are generally compatible. Your BR-R317 calipers will work fine with SM-RT81 rotors, RT30 and RT81 are both Ice Tech rotors with the same mounting and thickness.

You can keep using G03S pads. They are the correct resin pad for R317 and will bed in normally on RT81, no need to change pad model.

G02S is the older resin pad, G03S is the newer evolution with improved heat management and modulation. Both fit the same caliper, so your friend’s suggestion works, but G03S is the better current choice for your setup.

Strava accepts H.264 video in MP4 container with AAC audio. Use ffmpeg: ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -profile:v high -level 4.0 -crf 23 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 128k -movflags +faststart out.mp4. Keep resolution ≤1080p, 30fps, and file <1GB. Re-encode from action camera footage with these settings for reliable mobile upload and ensure audio sample rate 44.1kHz or 48kHz. Strava is picky about these.

Pre-made crepes reheat best gently, not microwaved, and cognac is flambéed with fresh crepes, not used to reheat frozen ones.

Thaw crepes in fridge overnight, then keep them covered with a damp paper towel. Warm a skillet over medium-low heat, add a knob of butter. Lay one crepe in, warm 30-45 seconds per side, just until pliable.

If you want cognac flavor, warm the crepe first, then remove to a plate. In the same pan add 1-2 tbsp cognac, let it bubble off alcohol for ~30 seconds, then spoon it over the crepe with sugar or cream.

Serve. This preserves texture and adds aroma without making the crepes soggy or boozy.

30 minutes on a hot gas grill will give you a good crust but very little smoke penetration. Smoke flavor is best absorbed at low temperatures over time, so a brief sear is mainly for color and texture.

With only a gas grill and chips, the best compromise is sous vide first, then a low-and-slow smoke finish. Preheat your grill with a smoker box or foil pouch of chips over one lit burner, keep the other burner off for indirect heat, and place the rack over the unlit side at 250-275F. 30-45 minutes will deposit noticeable smoke without overcooking the sous vide interior.

Finish with a 1-2 minute direct sear per side for crust. This gives you sous vide precision plus real smoke.

Commercial frozen fries are par-blanched, then frozen, and they are designed to be finished at a much higher temperature than 175C. At 175C you are essentially steaming the exterior starch before it can set crisp, and the par-cooked core releases a lot of water on contact with hot oil. That water flashes to steam, softens the crust you just formed, and the steam then gets trapped when you move them to a bowl.

First, dry the fries. Even though they are frozen, they collect surface ice crystals in the bag. Spread them on a tray and let them sit 5-10 minutes so the outside is dry, or pat them lightly. Wet fries = steam = soggy.

Second, finish hotter and faster. Most par-cooked frozen fries want 185-190C for the final crisp. 175C is a holding temp, not a crisping temp. Fry in a very small batch so the oil temperature does not drop more than 10-15C, and pull them when just golden, not pale. If your fryer cannot recover quickly, do two batches.

Third, drain properly. A wide bowl traps steam. Transfer immediately to a wire rack set over a sheet pan, not paper towels and not a bowl. The rack lets steam escape from both sides. Do not cover them.

Finally, serve immediately. Even perfect fries will soften if left to sit. If you must hold them, keep them warm in a 90C oven on a rack, not in the fryer basket. The oil you describe is probably fine, but make sure it is at the correct temperature with a thermometer, not the dial.

Yes, you can get the umami tingle without the oil bath. Lao Gan Ma’s flavor comes from fermented chili, soy, garlic and MSG, not the oil itself, so you can replicate it with almost no fat.

Try a low-oil chili crisp: toast 2 tbsp dried chili flakes with 1 tsp neutral oil, then immediately add 3 tbsp water, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tsp soy sauce or tamari, 1/2 tsp mushroom powder or miso, a pinch of sugar and a pinch of MSG. Simmer 2 min until thick. You get crunch, salinity and umami for ~15 calories per tablespoon.

Commercial oil-free bases work well: Huy Fong Chili Garlic Sauce and Sambal Oelek are salty, fermented and 0 fat. Mix them with toasted chili flakes and a tiny dash of sesame oil for aroma.

Use it as a finishing sprinkle rather than a drizzle. A little goes a long way on noodles, eggs or tofu, giving you the Old Godmother profile without hundreds of calories from soybean oil.

There is no reliable non-taste proxy for smoke flavor. Smoke deposition depends on wood species, moisture, airflow, temperature, and meat surface chemistry, not just time. Meats with more fat and surface area absorb more, and perception is delayed due to olfactory fatigue.

You can track process, not flavor: log wood type, chamber temp, meat surface temp, and total smoke exposure time. Use a smoke ring as a rough visual proxy for nitrogen dioxide uptake, but it correlates poorly with taste.

Best practice is standardized cook logs plus small test batches. Consistency beats quantification in practice today

Salt early and dry later. Salt the meat 40 minutes to 1 hour before cooking, then pat it completely dry. The salt draws moisture out, dissolves, and is reabsorbed, seasoning inside while the surface dries again. For dry-brining overnight, salt, refrigerate uncovered on a rack, and let the surface air-dry. Just before searing, pat off any excess moisture but not the salt. The crust forms from a dry surface, not unsalted meat. Seasoning stays in the meat, not on the pan. This gives flavor and a good sear.

Cherry tomatoes are usually safe if you remove the moldy one and the rest show no visible growth, but the situation you describe is risky. Mold spores spread in a sealed pack, and the black mold you saw can produce mycotoxins that are not removed by washing. The skin of cherry tomatoes is delicate and easily damaged, so contamination is possible.

For an inexpensive pack, the safest choice is to discard the whole lot. If you want to keep them, inspect each tomato carefully under light, discard any with blemishes, soft spots, or off smell, and wash thoroughly. Even then, risk is not zero.

The vinegar is almost certainly fine. Apple cider vinegar ferments to pH ~2.5-3.5, too acidic for microbes to thrive, and the alcohol stage kills most contaminants. A single fruit fly drowned months ago poses no food safety risk; it’s essentially pickled. If the liquid smells pleasantly sour-vinegary and not rotten or putrid, strain it through fine cloth and use it. When in doubt discard, but you likely don’t need to.

Crust is Maillard browning and caramelization, not frying by surface oil. High heat dehydrates the surface, causing proteins and sugars to brown and form a crust. Oil doesn't cause it; moisture loss does.

To avoid it, cook low and slow, keep the meat moist, cover with foil, or add steam and water to the pan. Sous vide then serve without searing also stays pale. Shop chops are often steamed or low-temp cooked then chilled, so they stay soft. Cutting the crust off works, but low heat preserves interior texture without browning.

First, safety over speed. Use your non-injured side for everything hot and heavy, and keep one hand free for stability. Wear a tight oven mitt on your good hand and use long tongs to keep distance from heat. A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath prevents slipping, and a rocking knife or a bench scraper lets you move food without gripping it.

Choose one-handed-friendly methods. Stovetop one-pot meals like veggie chilli, soups, and stews are ideal. Pre-chopped frozen veg, canned beans and tomatoes, and pre-minced garlic save chopping. Use a jar opener, electric can opener, and pull-tab packaging. Keep a countertop within arm’s reach for a “landing zone” so you never have to hold a hot pan while reaching.

For lifting, slide pans onto a trivet instead of carrying them, and use a lightweight saucepan. When stirring, anchor your elbow against your torso. Use a plate to transfer food instead of balancing bowls. Prep everything before you turn on heat, and use timers with loud alerts so you don’t have to watch constantly. Clean as you go in small batches to avoid a big mess later. Rest, and don’t try to rush.

Don't power a smoke detector from a wall switch; code requires continuous power. Install a proper smoke detector with battery backup or dedicated circuit. For lights, you can rewire at the fixture or junction box to make X and Y share switch B top. Turn off breaker, verify wires, connect X hot to Y hot. Blank A with a cover plate, but keep smoke detector powered and test before closing up.

That rattling on heat-up is classic for a one-pipe steam system, and the fact that it’s only your largest radiator is a big clue. It’s almost never the radiator “talking” normally; it’s something physically loose that gets excited when steam hits it.

On one-pipe steam the radiator fills from the bottom and steam enters at the bottom, so the whole body expands, water is pushed out, and the vent at the top closes. In a big old radiator that thermal shock and the sudden inrush of steam can make a loose internal part vibrate like a bell.

Most common causes:

1. Loose internal baffle or separator. Many large 1900s radiators have an internal baffle plate or a loose section of the first column that is no longer tightly riveted. When steam hits it, it rattles. You can sometimes hear it change tone as the radiator warms.

2. Loose radiator sections or a loose nipple. Old cast iron can work loose over decades. A small gap lets the section vibrate against its neighbor. The large radiator has more mass and more joints, so it’s more likely.

3. Loose mounting and piping. The radiator itself can be loose on its wall brackets, or the supply/return pipes can be inadequately supported. As the pipe heats it expands and bumps the wall or the radiator tee. Big radiators amplify that.

4. Vent chatter. A worn or incorrect vent can vibrate or rattle as it closes. One-pipe systems need a proper steam vent, not a water vent. A Gorton #1 or Hoffman #1 is typical. If someone put a fast-closing vent on, it can chatter.

What to do:

First isolate the sound. When it rattles, lightly touch the radiator sides and top with a gloved hand. If the vibration is localized to one column, that points to a loose internal part. Check that the radiator is firmly on its brackets and the bolts are tight. Look for pipe movement at the valve and near the wall; add pipe hangers or a short piece of insulation to keep it from hitting framing.

If you suspect the vent, replace it with a correct one-pipe steam vent in good condition, and make sure the radiator is pitched 1/4 in per foot toward the valve. That won’t fix a mechanical rattle but it helps overall operation.

For a true internal rattle you have two options: live with it, or have a radiator shop open the radiator and re-rivet or replace the loose baffle/section. That’s a job for a pro with steam experience.

Don’t tighten the bleed valve; it’s not the problem. If the sound is new, check for recent work that may have disturbed piping supports.

Yes, you can, but you need the correct drain assembly for the drain you have. What you’re looking at is a threaded bathtub waste with the original strainer and pop-up assembly removed. The visible threads are 1.5 in. nominal, which is standard for tubs, but the pop-up you tried is likely for a 1.75 in. or a different thread pitch, which is why it was too big.

You’ll need a replacement bathtub drain with a built-in pop-up and a 1.5 in. threaded tailpiece that mates to those existing threads. A universal lift-and-turn or push-pull pop-up drain, often sold as a ‘tub drain with strainer and pop-up’, will screw directly into the opening.

Remove any remaining gasket, clean the threads, screw the new strainer body in hand tight, then add plumber’s putty under the flange. The stopper mechanism is then set inside the strainer body. A simple strainer will fit, but a pop-up will work if you match the thread size.

Your proposed wiring would create two independent hot feeds to the same lamp string, which is unsafe and not code compliant. With the master switch closed the lights would be powered from the line side, and if the motion sensor also closes its contacts you would back-feed the line, creating a parallel supply and a shock hazard. The existing 3-way travelers are not suitable for this.

The motion sensor needs a neutral, and you cannot safely pull one from the switch loop without rewiring. The compliant way is to bring power to the fixture first, then feed the master switch and the motion sensor in parallel from that junction, and return their switched hots to the fixture. Use the existing 3-way cable to bring neutral and switched hot to the sensor box, or run new 14/3.

A better solution is a single-pole master switch in series with the motion sensor, or a motion sensor with built-in override, or a relay module at the first box so only one control path energizes the lamps.

Your 5/32" bit is correct for a 3/16" Tapcon, but hammer drilling often blows the hole out, especially in soft block, brick or crumbly concrete. The hammer action enlarges the hole beyond nominal size and dust packs the hole, giving zero bite.

Vacuum and brush the hole clean, then test the bit in fresh material. A worn or cheap bit can cut oversize, so use a new quality bit and try rotary only for the final pass.

If the hole is already wallowed, move 1/2" over. For a loose hole you can upsize to a 1/4" Tapcon with a 3/16" bit, or fill with epoxy anchor and re-drill.

Test button should work even without an equipment ground. The 'No Equipment Ground' label only means the receptacle isn't grounded, not that the GFCI is disabled. A functioning GFCI trips its internal test circuit regardless of ground. If the test button does nothing, the device is defective or miswired, not normal for ungrounded use. Replace it and have it checked by an electrician.

The fan is quiet on the bench because it isn’t coupled to anything. Installed, its vibration is transmitted to the ceiling box, drywall and ductwork, which act like a sounding board.

Check loose mounting screws, a housing not seated flat, or the box rattling against joists. A loose flex duct will flap and resonate. The old box may be warped.

Isolate the fan with rubber grommets, tighten fasteners, seal the duct connection, and ensure the housing isn’t touching metal. That stops the ceiling from amplifying normal noise.

Smart bulbs typically draw 0.3 to 1.5 W in standby when the switch stays on and the bulb is “off”. Most name-brand bulbs sit around 0.5-0.8 W, some budget models up to ~2 W.

For a 10 W LED used 6 h/day, active use is ~60 Wh/day. Standby for 18 h at 0.7 W is ~12.6 Wh/day, about 17% extra.

The LED still saves ~85-90% versus a 60 W incandescent, even with standby. The parasitic draw is real but small, usually a fraction of a watt, not enough to erase LED savings.

You have a classic double-hung storm window. The latches are called sash locks or storm window clips. Replace all four with matching spring latches from a hardware store or restoration supplier.

For water intrusion, reverse panel order so the lower sash overlaps the upper, or add a small drip cap/weep holes. Sealing the frame with butyl tape will also prevent rain from tracking behind the sashes and check the existing weatherstripping for gaps

NM cable cannot be fished through a 1/2 inch hole into flex metallic conduit. NM must enter a box through a listed clamp and cannot be run in FMC. FMC is not permitted to terminate into a non-metallic box unless the box and connector are listed for that use; bonding the far end does not make it compliant.

You cannot drywall over FMC. The conduit must be protected from nails and screws. Reroute it if possible, or install a nail plate over the run in the wall. A blank face plate only protects the box opening, not the wall cavity.

The box is likely overfilled. NEC requires box fill based on conductor volume, device and clamps. Four cables plus device yoke is almost certainly too much for a standard box. Crammed conductors overheat and are unsafe.

Replace the existing box with a deeper old-work box or add a junction box to reduce fill. Do not stuff NM into FMC or leave it unprotected.

The reflexive intensifies 'the monkey', not 'I'. The clause's subject is I, object is the monkey. Himself is an intensifier meaning 'the monkey himself', i.e. the monkey in person, not his image. The core is 'I showed the monkey', with himself adding emphasis. Subject and object remain distinct, so the usual co-reference rule is not violated. It is an emphatic use, parallel to 'I saw John himself' and is fully grammatical.

Most style guides treat the article as part of the formal title only when it is fixed in the name. Chicago Manual of Style and MLA capitalize The when it is integral to the title, e.g., The Duke of Wellington, The Prince of Wales, but lower-case it when it is a descriptive appositive, e.g., the duke of Wellington, the Prince of Wales. In running text the article is usually lowercased unless it begins a sentence or is part of a formal style. British practice, especially in Burke’s Peerage and Debrett’s, tends to capitalize The in formal lists of peerages. Consistency within a work matters more than absolute rule, so follow your chosen manual and apply it uniformly.

Yes, it happens. Common in military, sports, schools, and workplaces where formality or brevity is valued. Coaches call athletes by surname, teachers use last names for students. Also in close-knit groups as a sign of familiarity, or to show respect/distance. It can be affectionate or disciplinary, depending on tone and context.

Yes, "princesses'" is correct for the possessive plural, and it is pronounced /ˈprɪnsəsɪz/ with a final /ɪz/ sound, not silent.

Singular: princess /ˈprɪnsəs/. Possessive singular: princess's or princess' /ˈprɪnsəsɪz/ or /ˈprɪnsəs/. Both are attested, with princess's now preferred by most style guides.

Plural: princesses /ˈprɪnsəsɪz/. Possessive plural: princesses' /ˈprɪnsəsɪz/. The possessive marker is just an apostrophe added to an already plural form ending in s.

So the doll of one princess is a princess's doll or princess' doll.

The dolls belonging to many princesses is princesses' dolls. The final -es of the plural is pronounced, and the possessive apostrophe adds no extra sound; you do not get "princess-is-is". You get /ˈprɪnsəsɪz dɒlz/.

The confusion arises because the plural already ends in -es. For plurals ending in s, the possessive is formed by apostrophe only, with no additional syllable.

The process you describe is often called **belief perseverance with motivated rationalization**, or more colloquially a self-sealing belief system.

One entrenched false premise triggers motivated reasoning and confirmation bias: anomalies are explained away with ad hoc hypotheses, each new rationalization protects the core belief and creates further anomalies that require more rationalizations. The result is a cascading, self-reinforcing web of increasingly convoluted beliefs.

"Slam home" is an idiomatic intensifier meaning to make a point forcefully and unmistakably clear. It is a variant of "drive home" or "hammer home", with slam adding a sense of force and finality.

In non-sport use it means to stress, underline or emphasize an argument so it sticks. The report slams home the need for reform = the report makes the need unmistakable and impossible to ignore. Synonyms are drive home, hammer home, underline, emphasize, stress, press, nail down, make clear.

In sport, especially cricket and football, it is more literal: to slam the ball home means to strike it powerfully into the goal or net and score decisively. The phrase then carries connotations of force, accuracy and a clinching success.

Both uses share the core idea of emphatic, forceful delivery that leaves no room for doubt.

The phrase plays on the meal metaphor. The turkey is the main work, the effort you put in; gravy is the incidental extra that goes on top. Saying “the result is the gravy, not the turkey” means the outcome is secondary, a by-product, not the point of the work itself. It’s the opposite of “It’s all gravy,” which means extra profit or ease. Here the author stresses process over product: do the work well, the result will follow, don’t chase the result.

Yes, it can occur, but your example is not truly declarative. 'Please, can we request...' is a polite imperative request, not a statement. The clause 'can we request...' is interrogative in form but used as a softened directive.

True declarative use of can is rare. You can say 'Can be difficult' as reduced relative? Better: 'Can' as noun meaning ability. e.g., 'Can is important.' That's declarative.

So the period is correct, it's a request for politeness today.

The space you see before ! ? and “ is not English punctuation spacing at all, it is the French typographic tradition that was widely used in British book printing well into the early 20th century.

In France, and in much of Europe, a non-breaking space was set before  ? ! : ; » and sometimes before . The same convention was taught in British composing rooms and appears in Macmillan, Collins and many other London editions from the 1890s to the 1930s, even for English text. 

The practice began to disappear after the Second World War. Monotype and later phototypesetting, cheaper American house styles, and the post-war internationalisation of publishing removed the extra thin spaces. By the late 1950s British trade publishing had largely adopted the unspaced American model, so the spaced exclamation and question marks, and the spaced opening quote, are now read as pre-war.

Liberman's strip-of-land theory is clever but not definitive. The 1756 attestation is early, with no clear semantic bridge from 'strip' to 'jargon'. Romani, Scandinavian and Dutch snake theories remain plausible, and the French langue/lingo confusion is well documented. Etymology here is circumstantial; the prize problem persists because the earliest uses lack transparent cognates. More archival citations are needed before any single origin can be accepted as settled.

In both cases diplomatic corps were expelled, not interned. Britain and Germany exchanged personnel in September 1939: British minister Sir Nevile Henderson left Berlin on 3 Sept, German ambassador von Ribbentrop’s staff left London. They were given a few days to pack and travel via neutral Sweden or Portugal.

Similarly in December 1941 Japanese ambassador Nomura and staff were permitted to leave Washington under flag of truce, and US diplomats left Tokyo via Lisbon. Diplomacy functioned as reciprocal hostages, so expulsion was orderly and timed to avoid retaliation.

Street's Jorrocks was a proprietary brand of farmyard manure and later of artificial fertilisers sold in Britain from the late 19th century.

The name comes from the comic sporting squire Jorrocks, created by Robert Searle in the 1840s and popularised in Jorrocks’s Jaunts and Jollities. The character was a stereotypical, well-fed country gentleman, and his name became a generic byword for rustic, hearty farm life.

Street & Co. of London marketed Jorrocks as a complete manure and feeding compound for livestock, especially pigs and poultry, with a distinctive striped sack and Jorrocks’s likeness on it. By the Second World War the brand was ubiquitous on British farms.

Hastings uses it as shorthand for the everyday, low-tech reality of wartime agriculture: farmers were still relying on old commercial manures like Street’s Jorrocks rather than modern mechanisation, reflecting chronic under-investment, labour shortage and the makeshift nature of British farming in the 1940s.

There is no single published roster with full service dates for 300 Squadron. The best sources are archival: The National Archives, Kew holds Operations Record Books AIR 27/1124-1130 covering personnel movements, missions and casualties. The Polish Institute and Sikorski Museum in London holds squadron personnel files and the ‘Księga Cmentarza’ card index. The Polish Air Force Memorial at Northolt and the website 300sqn.pl compile partial nominal rolls from ORBs. For individual service histories consult the Central Military Archives in Warsaw, Archiwum Akt Nowych, and the Institute of National Remembrance personnel records. These must be consulted in person.

No. English law never criminalised a mere slip in form of address to the monarch. Lèse-majesté and seditious libel required intent to defame, threaten or deny authority, not an accidental 'Your Royal Highness' instead of 'Your Majesty'. Prosecutions needed clear words of contempt, denial of right, or incitement. A formal mistake, however discourteous, was social faux pas, not a punishable crime. Courts demanded seditious meaning, not etiquette breaches, throughout the early modern period.

The cap with “12” and blue-grey tunic matches the French 12th Infantry Regiment, circa 1870s. Tampico was a common entry point for French veterans after the Franco-Mexican War and later for French Foreign Legion recruits. He likely served in France before emigrating to Mexico.

Maize dominated because it fit the ecology, economy and culture of eastern and midwestern North America far better than Old World cereals did for centuries.

Maize is a high-yielding C4 plant that thrives in hot, humid summers and tolerates poor, acidic soils of the eastern woodlands where wheat and rye struggle. It can be planted late, harvested over months, and stored as dried ears. It also provided a complete subsistence package: corn for bread and hominy, stalks for fodder, and a reliable calorie base for dense populations.

When wheat arrived after 1492, it required drier, cooler summers, better-drained soils and a longer growing season with winter dormancy. In the humid South and Appalachia wheat rusted badly; in the Upper Midwest the growing season was too short until the late 19th century. Experience mattered too: generations of knowledge about planting, selection and processing maize was embedded in farm practice.

Wheat only became universal after railroad transport, steel plows, and fallow rotations opened the semi-arid Great Plains in the 1870s-1890s, and after global markets made wheat an export cash crop. Before then maize was the local staple and industrial feedstock for whiskey and later livestock.

Corn was used in beer, though less than barley. Early brewers used corn as a cheap adjunct for body and fermentable sugar, a practice that persisted in corn beer and later in bourbon whisky.

Pieces of eight were not cut with specialized tools but with whatever was at hand. Spanish colonial silver was relatively soft, about 90% silver, so a sharp blow could split it. Travelers and merchants commonly used a knife, a hatchet, or a chisel on a hard surface like a stone or an anvil. In shops a hammer and a chopping block sufficed; in the field a machete or even a rock was used. Some cutters made a notch first to guide the break, then struck along the lines to produce eight wedge-shaped bits, each a real. Blacksmiths were not required, though they could do a cleaner job. The resulting irregular pieces were weighed when exact value mattered, making cutting practical for everyday small change.

Yes, it was possible, though unusual, and it depended on the officer’s status and the circumstances.

A commissioned officer in the Royal Navy held a commission from the Crown, not an appointment to a particular ship. He was on the Navy List and could be unemployed between appointments, a state called being on half-pay. While unemployed he was a gentleman officer, not a seaman, and could travel as a passenger on any vessel, merchant or otherwise, at his own expense. On furlough or leave, there was no regulation forbidding travel on a civilian ship; indeed, many officers used merchant packets, East Indiamen, or even private yachts to get to and from ports, especially when the Navy had no transport available.

The more interesting case is an officer sailing under commission on a non-warship. In wartime the Admiralty regularly commissioned non-rate vessels for naval duties. Sloops, cutters, hired armed ships, and even converted merchantmen were put on the Navy List and commissioned with a Royal Navy commander or lieutenant in charge. The officer was then officially on a naval vessel, even if it was a former merchant hull. Hired armed ships were a particular example: private merchant vessels taken on short-term charter for convoy escort, carrying men and guns under a naval commission. A first lieutenant could very well find himself serving on one of these.

Officers also served on royal yachts, receiving ships, hospital ships, and transport vessels. The Royal Navy operated a fleet of transports for moving troops and stores, and they were commanded by naval officers. Likewise, a lieutenant could be appointed to a survey vessel, a tender, or a small despatch boat.

There is also the case of acting appointments and temporary duty. An officer waiting for a ship might be sent as a passenger on a merchant vessel to reach a station where a vacancy existed, with the Admiralty’s approval, and would be paid passage money. This was not service, but it was common practice.

What would be almost unthinkable is a commissioned officer taking a subordinate role on a purely civilian merchant ship for pay. A captain or lieutenant would not serve as a merchant master or mate under a merchant owner; it would be a loss of status and a breach of professional etiquette. If he did so, he would do so as a passenger or as a private gentleman, not as a naval officer on duty.

So, in short: on leave, yes, he could travel on a civilian ship as a passenger. On duty, he could only serve on a vessel commissioned by the Crown, which in the 18th century often included hired armed merchantmen and other non-rate craft, not private trading vessels.

The portrait you describe is almost certainly not a regular British Army uniform, and the details you give make a colonial civil or paramilitary service much more likely.

George Anderson born 1856 in Kildare would be in his late teens to mid-20s in the mid to late 1870s to 1880s, the typical age for a studio carte-de-visite or cabinet card of that kind. Men who emigrated or worked intermittently in South Africa in that period rarely wore a British line infantry tunic. The cut you are describing, with a dark double-breasted tunic, high collar, plain peaked cap and a belt with a large oval or rectangular buckle, matches the civilianised uniforms adopted by colonial police and railway and mining companies in the Cape Colony and Natal in the 1870s-1880s.

The Natal Police, formed in 1849 and expanded in the 1870s, and the Cape Mounted Police later Cape Colonial Police, wore a dark blue or black tunic with red piping, brass buttons, and a peaked cap with a black band. Many private employers in South Africa, especially the Witwatersrand mining firms and the Natal Government Railways, issued essentially the same dark service dress to clerks, guards and overseers, often with a company badge on the cap and a plain waist belt.

If the tunic has a high standing collar, no regimental facings and a plain cap with a company or police badge rather than a military cap badge and shako or busby, it is the uniform of a colonial police constable or a railway/mining company employee, the kind of work that would bring an Irish-born man to South Africa for seasonal employment. It is not a British Army or Irish Constabulary dress, which would have distinct facing colours, a different headgear and more elaborate buttons.

To confirm you would need a clear view of the buttons and cap badge. A police or company badge would be oval with the name of the colony or company, whereas a military badge would be a crown over crossed items.

Robert Briscoe died on Thursday 29 May 1969 in Dublin, and was buried on 31 May 1969.

The confusion is a classic case of death date vs. reporting and burial date getting conflated. The contemporaneous Irish press reports the death on the evening of 29 May. The Irish Press, 30 May 1969, p. 1, reports: “Mr Robert Briscoe, TD, died yesterday evening.” The Irish Times obituary on 30 May 1969 also gives “died yesterday”. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency dispatch dated 30 May 1969 wires “Irish Jewish leader Robert Briscoe dies at 74”, and the Dictionary of Irish Biography records the death as 29 May 1969.

The 30 May date that appears on the German Wikipedia, Haaretz and elsewhere is the date the death was publicly announced and reported in the press. The 31 May date given by the Palgrave Dictionary of Anglo-Jewish History is the date of his funeral and burial at Mount Jerome Cemetery, Dublin, which was held on Saturday 31 May 1969.

No reliable contemporary source gives a precise time of day. Newspaper reports only specify “yesterday evening” / “last night”. The Irish Press says he died at his home, 12 Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin, after a long illness, in the evening of 29 May. The exact hour is not recorded in the obituaries or death notice consulted.

Yes, for mortgage underwriting. Lenders treat 401(k) loan repayments as a monthly debt obligation even though it doesn’t appear on credit reports. The payment is verified on paystubs and included in DTI calculations. It counts until fully repaid, regardless of FICO visibility and most lenders will require written documentation of the repayment schedule.

Stock price reflects expectations, not just reported numbers. Analyst estimates are already priced in, so the market reacts to the surprise and what it implies for the future.

Beating EPS by 10% does not mean a 10% price rise. EPS is one metric; investors also weigh revenue, margins, guidance, cash flow, and the quality of earnings. A beat achieved by cost cuts or one-time items can be negative.

Often the market had already anticipated the beat, or the company issues weak forward guidance, which overshadows the good quarter. Prices move on revisions to future earnings expectations, not past results alone. That is why a beat can still lead to a decline.

Yes, you can occasionally get coins and notes worth more than face value from circulation, but it is neither easy nor reliable, and you will not make a fortune this way.

Modern Eisenhower dollars are a good example. Most circulated pieces are common and worth about $1 to $2. The rare 1972 Type 2 with a doubled die obverse, or a 1971-S proof, can be worth hundreds, but those are not found in bank teller rolls. Banks do not sort for numismatic value, and the chance of pulling a true rarity from random circulation is tiny.

Where it does happen is with older coins that have been lost in circulation for decades. Wheat cents, silver war nickels, pre-1965 silver dimes and quarters, and some error coins still turn up occasionally. Paper money is even harder; modern Federal Reserve notes are rarely worth more than face unless uncirculated, star notes, or a rare serial number.

You can improve odds by checking rolls from banks, asking for older coins, and learning to identify key dates and errors. That is a hobby, not an investment strategy. The numismatic market is efficient; anything truly valuable is quickly removed from circulation by collectors and dealers.

In short, it is possible to get lucky, it is not easy, and it will not make you rich. Treat it as a fun search with a small upside, not a way to build wealth.

With a 100 euro account and 50:1 leverage you are not trading with 100 euros, you are controlling a 5,000 euro position. That is the point and the danger.

Going long with leverage you do not owe the broker more than your deposit in theory, but you can still lose the 100 euros very quickly and be liquidated. DeGiro will close your position on a margin call once your equity falls below the maintenance requirement, typically around 25-30% of the margin used. With 50:1 that is a ~2% adverse move in the stock and your account is wiped.

The phrase “you never lose more than your initial position” is true only if the broker liquidates before negative equity occurs. In practice gaps, slippage on volatile stocks, and delayed execution can mean you are liquidated at a worse price than your stop, or the stop is never filled. You still lose only the 100 euros, but you cannot count on a perfect exit.

If you really want to limit loss to 100 euros:

Use position sizing, not leverage ratio. Decide a max loss per trade, e.g. 2% of account = 2 euros. With 50:1 leverage a 2 euro loss corresponds to a ~0.04% move in the underlying, so you must trade a tiny nominal exposure. On a 100 euro account that means maybe 20-40 euros nominal exposure, not 5,000.

Never use the full 50:1. Treat leverage as a tool for position size, not as a target.

Use hard stop-loss orders and accept they can gap through. For a 100 euro account, use highly liquid large caps and avoid earnings days.

Keep leverage positions short term and monitor intraday. Overnight gaps are where small accounts die.

Most importantly, paper trade the mechanics first. Real money with leverage is emotionally different, but 100 euros will be gone in one bad gap and you will learn nothing except how fast it can happen.

Under ERISA a 401k plan amendment that reduces accrued benefits is a cut-back amendment. It can be made prospective only and cannot reduce benefits already accrued.

Your accrued benefit as of the amendment date is protected. Vesting is a form of accrued benefit. Changing vesting from 3 to 6 years for service already completed in 2019 is a cut-back.

ERISA §204(h) requires the plan sponsor to give participants notice at least 30 days before the effective date of any amendment that reduces accrued benefits, including a change to a less favorable vesting schedule.

Notice sent 24 Nov 2019 for a change that applies to 2019 is both untimely and retroactive. A plan amendment cannot apply retroactively to service already performed.

Contact the plan administrator in writing and request the Summary of Material Modifications and the plan amendment document. If the change is being applied retroactively to your accrued benefit, file a complaint with the Department of Labor EBSA.

Compare on an annualized holding period return, not just absolute rupee gain.

You paid 5,000. Selling now at 9,750 gives a total gain of 4,750, or 95% cumulative. Holding to 12-Nov-2020 gives maturity proceeds of 10,800 plus all 8% coupons received since purchase. The cumulative gain is 5,800 plus coupons.

Annualise both: HPR = (Ending value / Beginning value)^(1/years) -1. For sale now use current market price as ending value and actual holding period. For maturity use 10,800 plus accrued coupons as ending value and full holding period.

If the annualised return from holding to maturity, including reinvested coupons, exceeds the annualised return from selling now and redeploying proceeds, holding is better. Market price already reflects yield to maturity.

Yes, it is possible to retain your UK pay level when moving to another EU country, but it is the exception rather than the rule and it depends entirely on your employer’s policy, the nature of your role, and how the move is structured.

Most large multinationals do have internal precedents for this. The usual models are:

1. Home country pay retention with a cost-of-living adjustment. This is common for short-term international assignments, typically 1-3 years. Your base salary is maintained in GBP, often with a COLA or hardship allowance added or removed to reflect the destination. You remain on the UK payroll or on an assignment payroll, and you are usually covered by the home country benefits. The employer is essentially paying a premium to keep you, and the assignment has a defined end date and a repatriation plan.

2. Global grade / global band retention. Some companies, especially in tech, finance and consulting, use a global grading structure. If your role is truly global, client facing, or revenue generating for the UK entity, they may keep you on the UK grade and pay you in GBP even if you are physically in, say, Poland, Portugal or the Czech Republic. This is more likely if you continue to report to a UK manager, work UK hours, and serve UK clients. The employer will usually justify it as “market rate for the role, not for the location”.

3. Local hire with salary mapping. This is the default for a permanent relocation. You are employed by the local legal entity and paid according to the local pay structure. Companies will often run a salary mapping exercise, comparing your UK grade to the local grade, and may offer a retention premium for a transition period, e.g. 12-24 months, to avoid a cliff edge. After that, your pay moves to local increments.

Precedent exists but it is not automatic. The key factors that make retention more likely are:

Role scarcity and replaceability. If you are in a specialist, high demand skill set that is hard to hire locally at the local market rate, you have leverage. The employer can calculate the cost of recruiting and onboarding someone new versus paying you a premium.

Continuity of employer and tax. If you remain employed by the UK entity and are seconded, the employer avoids creating a new employment contract and social security registration in the destination country. That is simpler administratively but creates permanent establishment and social security risks for the employer, so they prefer it to be temporary.

Destination country. Non-Euro countries such as Poland, Hungary, Czechia, Romania and Sweden have a much larger cost-of-living and salary differential with the UK than, for example, Denmark or the Netherlands. The gap makes retention harder to justify internally. HR will be asked why a UK salary is being paid for a job done in a lower-cost market.

How to make it work. Frame the request as a business case, not a personal preference. Show that the role can be performed remotely or from the destination without loss of output. Propose a structure, e.g. keep UK base, accept local benefits, or accept a phased reduction. Get written agreement on tax treatment, pension continuity, and whether you will be on UK payroll with a local tax equalisation policy.

In practice, permanent relocation with full pay retention is rare outside of senior leadership or truly global roles. More common is a hybrid: retain base for a defined period, then transition to local rates with a top-up. If you need the UK pay level indefinitely, you will likely need to negotiate a remote working arrangement where you remain UK based for employment purposes, which brings its own visa and tax complications.

Speak to your HR mobility team early. Ask specifically about international assignment policy, salary harmonisation, and precedent cases for your grade.

Yes, you can re-apply, and in practice you almost certainly should not wait for the existing offer to expire if rates have fallen.

A mortgage offer in the UK is not a binding contract until you accept it and complete. The offer is just a conditional agreement valid for a set period, typically 3-6 months, sometimes up to 6 months. Until you accept it and draw down the mortgage, you are free to do nothing, let it lapse, or make a new application.

You can apply with the same lender for a new offer. Most lenders will simply cancel or supersede the old offer and issue a new one at current rates and criteria. Because you already have a credit search on file, the process is usually quicker, but it will still involve a fresh affordability assessment and a new hard credit search. That new search will show up on your credit file and could affect your score in the short term, though the impact is modest.

You can also apply with a different lender. There is no restriction on having multiple live offers, though you should be mindful of multiple credit searches in a short period. Under the soft vs hard search rules, mortgage searches from the same window are usually grouped by credit reference agencies, so the impact is limited if you use a whole of market broker and apply within ~14-30 days.

Implications to consider:

* **Rate lock:** The old offer locks you to the rate at the time it was made. If rates have fallen, you are financially worse off keeping it.
* **Valuation:** A new application will require a fresh valuation, usually at your cost, £150-£300. The old valuation may be out of date if property prices have moved or the lender's policy changed.
* **Criteria change:** Lender affordability rules, income multiples and product criteria change over time. Re-applying means you will be assessed against current rules, which may be tighter or looser.
* **Offer expiry:** Letting the old offer expire naturally is fine, but do not complete on it if you want a better rate. Once you accept the offer and complete, you cannot renegotiate.

Practical steps: Contact your current lender, tell them you wish to withdraw the existing offer and request a re-quote at today's rates. Ask if they will honour the original valuation or if a new one is needed. If you are using a broker, instruct them to do a fresh market comparison now. Do not accept the old offer until you have compared the new rate.

If you are close to completion, check your exchange of contracts date and the seller's patience, as re-valuation can add a few days.

US citizens and green card holders are taxed on worldwide income no matter where they live, so moving to Taiwan does not create a general exemption from US tax.

The US$70,000 figure you recall is the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion, which in 2024 is $126,500. It applies only to earned income from work, not to retirement income. Social Security, interest, dividends and capital gains are unearned and are not covered by the FEIE.

Your Social Security benefits may be taxable in the US depending on provisional income, up to 85% of benefits. Interest and dividends are fully taxable as ordinary income and qualified dividends, and capital gains are taxable at 0/15/20% depending on your taxable income.

You can reduce tax with the standard deduction, $14,600 for single filers in 2024, and with the Foreign Tax Credit if Taiwan taxes you, but Taiwan generally does not tax foreign-source pension, interest, dividends or capital gains of non-residents.

There is no special retirement exemption for living in Taiwan.

The “void after 90 days” is a bank policy, not a legal expiration of the debt. A check can still be paid after that date if the issuer honors it, but most banks will reject a 6-year-old check and the title company will almost certainly stop payment on it.

In Oregon the statute of limitations for a contract debt is generally 6 years. You are right at that limit, so waiting to pursue it is risky. The better move is to contact the title company directly, explain you just found an uncashed closing check for $38, and ask for a reissue or a refund via ACH/check.

Provide the closing file number, property address and the check number. Ask them to confirm the balance is still outstanding and to issue a new payment. Keep a written record of the request.

Depositing the old check is unlikely to work and can create a delay if the bank flags it as stale-dated.

At six, musical joy matters more than progress. Forcing violin is teaching her that learning equals stress and shame, and bad habits now will be hard to unlearn later. The community is lovely, but she’s already associating it with pressure. Let her stop with kindness, keep music alive through singing and listening, and leave the door open. She may return later by choice, not coercion.

Single communal bedroom sounds ideal in theory but runs into practical and developmental realities.

Sleep needs differ: teens need 8-9 hours but often go to bed later than younger kids, and light/noise sensitivity makes shared sleep hard. One child’s nightmare, illness, or early wake-up disrupts all.

Privacy is crucial. Preteens and teens need a private space to decompress, manage emotions, try identities, and have conversations with friends or partners. Without it they may withdraw elsewhere.

Boundaries and conflict increase with proximity. Sibling rivalry, differing temperature, music, study habits, and mess tolerance become friction points with no escape valve.

Health and hygiene: shared airspace increases transmission of colds, and items get lost or misused.

Finally, communal sleeping can blur parental boundaries. Normalizing sex is good, but children still need a space free from parental and sibling observation for bodily autonomy and dignity.

A family room for bonding plus individual sleep spaces balances connection and respect.

At 3 years 2 months, screaming when things go wrong is communication, not defiance. She has limited language and big feelings, so screaming is her loudest tool when she feels frustrated, thwarted, or overwhelmed. Teaching phrases is great, but it takes much longer than a few weeks for a new skill to replace an old one under stress.

First, lower the stakes before the meltdown. For small frustrations like a toy not sitting right or an iPad freezing, narrate and model calm problem solving out loud: “Teddy fell. That’s frustrating. I can help you fix it.” Keep your voice low and slow. If she screams, stay nearby, stay calm, and wait for a pause. Then offer a simple choice she can control: “Do you want help or do you want space?”

For bigger transitions like leaving the park, prepare ahead. Give a clear, brief preview with a visual cue: “First park, then home. After home, snacks.” Use a consistent goodbye ritual, like a special wave or a song, so the ending is predictable. When she protests, acknowledge the feeling without negotiating the decision: “You wanted to go around the block. Now we’re going home. I know that’s hard.”

Don’t try to reason, threaten, or distract in the moment. She can’t access those inputs while flooded. Safety first: if she is in danger, hold her firmly and calmly and say “I’m keeping you safe.” 

Pick one tiny moment a day to practice a replacement. When she is calm, play “help me” with toys and praise any attempt. Over months, consistency builds the pathway so help-seeking becomes easier than screaming.

First, you are not failing as a stepparent. You are in an almost impossible position: limited contact, no communication with the treatment team, no integration into her life when you arrived, and a spouse who is neutral. That is not a foundation for a therapeutic relationship, and it is not fair to expect you to fix it alone.

With a 16 year old diagnosed with Reactive Attachment Disorder, aggression is often not defiance but fear, hypervigilance, and a learned expectation that adults will be rejecting or controlling. Scream responses to requests like cleaning a room are protective, not personal. That does not make it okay for you to be targeted, but it does change what will help.

Given your limited time, 20-60 minutes a day, and the lack of access to her therapist, your role should be small, consistent, and non-coercive. Do not try to parent, discipline, or therapize her. You cannot be the primary attachment figure and you do not have the clinical information or authority to do so.

Pick one low-stakes, predictable interaction and keep it boringly reliable. A brief hello, a shared snack, a short walk to the bus, or sitting in the same room while she does homework without talking. No requests, no corrections, no teaching moments. Predictability builds safety more than rapport does.

Use neutral, brief language when you must make a request. Keep it to one sentence, no justification or negotiation. "Shoes go in the closet." Then disengage. If she screams, do not match volume or argue. A calm "I hear you are upset. I will be in the kitchen." and leave the space is protective for both of you. You are modeling regulation, not winning.

Protect your own boundaries. It is reasonable to step away when she is aggressive toward you. "I am not going to stay when I am being yelled at. I will be back in 10 minutes." Consistency matters more than frequency.

You cannot be integrated into treatment without consent and coordination. Since the former in-laws pay and the therapist does not communicate with you, you should not push for access. That will likely increase her distrust of you as an extension of a parental conflict.

Do talk privately with your spouse, not about what you should do with her, but about what you need. "I want to be kind to her and I also need to feel safe in our home. Can we agree on a plan for when she is aggressive with me?" If your spouse remains neutral, that is information about the limits of support you can expect.

You have skills with children, but this child is not your student. Your professional rapport skills can help you stay calm, but do not import them here. The healthiest involvement for you right now is to be a calm, non-demanding presence and a safe adult who does not try to earn her love or fix her.

If aggression escalates to threats, property destruction, or safety concerns, document it and ask your spouse to raise it with the treatment team. You are a witness, not the case manager.

You can care without taking responsibility for her recovery.

First, congratulations on noticing and caring enough to ask. Being a guardian is already a big responsibility, and noticing a child is both brilliant and struggling socially is an important observation.

Please do not label him or her a genius, and please do not treat him or her like a normal kid either. Treat him like a 6 year old who is a unique individual. Age-appropriate emotional and social needs do not change because of cognitive ability. He still needs play, safety, rest, routine, affection, and time to be a child.

What you are describing is common for gifted children, especially those who have experienced trauma or instability. Advanced verbal and conceptual ability can coexist with underdeveloped social skills, delayed emotional regulation, and a very real need for peer connection. The fact that he cannot make friends is just as important as the fact that he solved a chemistry problem. One does not cancel out the other.

Your degree in chemistry is a gift to him, but it can also be a risk if it becomes the only way you connect. Children learn that love is conditional on performance very quickly. Keep the explanations you give curious and playful, but do not make intellectual stimulation the core of your relationship.

Get a professional evaluation, not to label him, but to get support. Ask your pediatrician for a referral to a psychologist who works with gifted and twice-exceptional children. A comprehensive assessment can look at cognitive abilities, language, social-emotional development, and any effects of prior neglect or trauma. That gives you a roadmap, not a trophy.

In the meantime, protect childhood. Provide access to age-appropriate play, movement, and unstructured time. Find one or two consistent, kind peer interactions rather than forcing a crowd. A small group, a mentor, a library story hour, a science club for elementary ages, or a shared interest activity can help him practice friendship skills without pressure.

Also protect him from adults. Do not parade him as a prodigy at work or online. That is exploitative and can damage his self-concept and safety. His ideas are his, not yours to showcase.

Finally, check your own expectations. You are likely proud and a little awed. That is normal. Make sure your pride does not become pressure. He does not need to become a chemist. He needs to feel safe, loved, and seen as a whole child.

You are doing well by asking. Keep seeking guidance from professionals, and keep him grounded in being six.

Clouds do not make UV safe, especially in NZ where UV is extreme. A UV index of 11-12 is extreme even on an overcast day. Up to 80% of UV penetrates thin cloud and is scattered sideways, so your baby can still receive significant exposure without direct sun.

Pram covers and positioning help but are not sufficient. Most fabrics transmit UV and a canopy gives only partial shade. Babies under 6 months should avoid direct sun entirely.

Best practice is to keep baby in full shade, ideally indoors during peak UV 10am-4pm. Use a broad-brimmed hat, UPF50+ clothing and a pram with a UPF-rated canopy. If you must go out, keep the time short. For infants over 6 months, use mineral sunscreen on exposed areas and reapply regularly.

The lockdown didn’t create a new kid, it created new conditions. At home, with no rush to school, no handover to daycare or grandparents, and a lot of low-pressure time together, your son felt safe enough to talk. The goal isn’t to recreate lockdown, it’s to keep that feeling of safety when life speeds up again.

First, drop the interrogation. Questions like “who did you play with at gym?” feel like a quiz and put him on the defensive. Kids shut down when they feel they are being monitored. Instead, offer observations and wait. “You looked tired after school today” or “That math worksheet was messy” gives him an opening without demanding a report.

Second, protect a short, predictable, no-agenda window. Five to ten minutes of real one-to-one time every day beats a longer, sporadic session. The bedtime moment you already noticed is gold. Keep phones out, keep lights low, and don’t problem-solve. Just listen and reflect: “That sounds frustrating” is enough. If he says nothing, that’s fine too.

Third, use the activities you already have. The morning cuddle and the evening tooth-brushing are already yours. Keep them calm and comment-free most of the time, then occasionally share something small about your day first. Modeling vulnerability invites reciprocity.

Finally, let him lead the timing. He told you things right before sleep because his guard is down then. Don’t chase the conversation in the car or at the dinner table. When he offers a piece, receive it without praise or fixing, and let him know you’ll be there the next time he wants to talk. Trust builds slowly, and it stays when you don’t push it.

Your daughter is not telling a story about ghosts, she is telling you she is scared and she needs you to be the safe adult who helps her make sense of it. At three, the line between imagination, memory and fear is very thin, and children often report frightening experiences in concrete, literal images like a black doll with no face or legs.

First, stay calm and validate, don’t debate the reality of the doll. In the moment she is terrified, reassurance and co-regulation matter more than explanations. Get down to her level, hold her, and say something like “That sounds really scary. I’m here. You are safe with me.” Do not dismiss it as “just pretend” or try to prove there is nothing there while she is panicked.

Later, when she is calm, explore the fear gently and curiously. Ask open, non-leading questions: “Can you show me where you saw it? What was it doing? What did it make you feel?” Keep it short and let her lead. Many three-year-olds confabulate details from a passing image, a shadow, a dream, or a comment they overheard. The repeated mention of a black doll staring at you while you sleep suggests it may be tied to a specific memory, a toy, a picture, or even a dream she is trying to place.

Create safety in the environment tonight. Sleep with her in your room or bring her bed to yours for a few nights if needed. Keep the night light on, keep the bathroom door open or closed consistently, and walk through the room with her during the day pointing out what is real. A simple bedtime routine with a predictable story, cuddle, and a “safe word” she can use if she is scared helps restore a sense of control.

Avoid introducing ghost or monster concepts if she doesn’t already know them, and don’t bring in scary explanations or investigations. If the fear persists, is interfering with sleep, appetite or play for more than a couple of weeks, or she keeps describing the same figure, check in with her pediatrician to rule out sleep issues, stress, or sensory sensitivities.

You are not failing her by taking this seriously. She is learning from you that fear can be named, contained, and soothed.

At two, hitting in the car is usually seeking sensation, attention, or just exploring reach, not meanness. Yelling and asking rarely works because the car is exciting and they can’t see the impact.

First, change the setup. Swap your 5-year-old and 2-year-old so the toddler is in the middle with the infant on one side and the 5-year-old on the other, or put the 2-year-old behind the driver where you can see him. A simple seat divider or a rolled towel barrier on the 5-year-old’s seat can block kicks without harming anyone.

Make the rule concrete and brief: “Feet on floor, hands to self.” Practice at home in the parked car with a toy reward for keeping feet down for 2 minutes, then build up.

Give a job: a window watcher chart, a special car-only toy, or a squeeze ball for his hands. If he kicks, calmly pull over safely, unbuckle, and give a short time-out on your lap. Consistency beats volume, and removing the audience and the opportunity stops the pattern.

Six months old is peak exploratory phase, and hands go straight to anything interesting, especially when it’s warm and moving. You don’t need to restrain him, you just need to make the grab less rewarding and the clean-up easier.

First, change the timing. If you know he grabs as soon as the diaper opens, do the reveal in stages. Keep the diaper on, wipe the outside, then only open the front a little while you talk and distract him with your voice, a song, or a high-contrast toy held just above his chest. Once his attention is up, you can lift and clean.

Second, give his hands a job. A small soft washcloth, a silicone teether, or even a clean muslin square clipped to the changing table gives him something to hold that isn’t his genitals. Offer it before you open the diaper and keep it in his hands during the clean.

Third, make cleanup faster. A warm wet washcloth on the area before you fully open the diaper softens stool and reduces the need for prolonged contact. A second small towel on your lap lets you catch mess without needing both hands free.

This is normal self-exploration, not a habit to punish. Brief, calm redirection and a little distraction are enough, and the phase usually passes in a few weeks.
