At three months this is very common and usually not a sign of a problem. Babies are developing hand awareness and will bat at anything near their face, including a bottle. That does not mean they are done eating.

The pattern you describe — sucking for a few seconds, then fussing and pushing the bottle away, then seeming hungry again minutes later — sounds more like a pause to breathe, swallow, and reset, rather than satiety. Newborns and infants often need breaks during a feed. The push away, a pause, then resuming is typical.

Teething is unlikely at three months. Babies do not get their first tooth until around 6 months, and teething discomfort usually comes with other signs like drooling, gum rubbing, and sleep changes.

Try offering smaller, more frequent feeds with breaks. Keep a calm environment, pause when he pushes, and gently re-offer the nipple when he calms. If he consistently takes less and remains fussy, check nipple flow, temperature, and positioning. If weight gain is good and diapers are normal, you can relax; otherwise check with your pediatrician.

You cannot motivate someone from the outside, especially not a 20-something who is anxious, low in self-esteem and already brittle with the family. Motivation that comes from pressure tends to turn into shame, and shame is what keeps her inside watching dramas and reading.

What you can do is change the conditions around her so that action becomes less threatening and less loaded.

First, stop making life-plans the topic of conversation. Every talk about work, future, university becomes a referendum on her failure in her mind. Pick a neutral, low-stakes domain. Invite her for a walk, a coffee, to help with a small household task, with no agenda attached. Rebuild safety before you rebuild ambition.

Second, get professional help, gently and concretely. The pattern you describe — extreme introversion, anxiety outside the home, depressive spans, brittle aggression inside — is not laziness. It is likely anxiety/depression, possibly with social anxiety. Offer one specific option, not a lecture: “I found a therapist who does online appointments for young adults. Would you be willing to try one session with me just to see what it’s like? I’ll pay.” If she refuses, leave the door open and don’t chase.

Third, lower the bar for “life experience” to something achievable this week. Not “get an apprenticeship”. Try “step outside for 10 minutes with me”. “Send one text to a friend”. Success builds self-efficacy; grand plans destroy it.

Fourth, protect the family system. With your wife, agree on a united, calm approach: no ultimatums, no comparisons to peers, no “time is running out” speeches. Those statements are true for you, but they are experienced by her as attack.

She has had opportunities and rejected them because the cost felt too high. Your job now is not to push her out the door, but to make the door less scary to open. That is slower than you want, but it is the only way to avoid breaking the family while you wait for her to be ready.

At 20 months this is completely normal. Pronouns are abstract and children typically master them between 2 and 3 years old, with you/me often being one of the last to solidify because they require understanding perspective-taking.

Correction alone can be frustrating for both of you. Try modeling in context rather than correcting in isolation. Use lots of physical cues and repetition. Point to yourself and say “Read to me” while touching your chest, then point to her and say “Read to you” while touching her chest, keeping the intonation warm and playful.

Make it a game with two clear roles. Hold up two identical books and say “This book is for you” handing it to her, and “This book is for me” holding it to your chest. Narrate your own actions: “Mama is drinking. Mama wants water. Give water to me.” Then offer her a cup: “Do you want water? Drink for you.”

Avoid over-correcting every utterance. Children learn pronouns best through meaningful, repeated use in routines. Bedtime, meals, and play are perfect. The more she hears you consistently use me for yourself and you for her in real interactions, the faster the concept will click.

She’s on track, just give her time.

Yes, you can fly directly to Kentucky. Your immigrant visa is valid for entry anywhere in the US. The address you gave on forms is not binding; it only helps USCIS with initial processing. You must still intend to reside permanently with your petitioner in Minnesota, and you should update your address with USCIS after arrival using AR-11. A short visit to family is fine for you.

Liechtenstein is essentially unique. Monaco has no domestic rail service either – all passenger trains run between France and Italy and merely stop in Monaco – but the service is operated by SNCF and Trenitalia as international through services. No other sovereign state with regular passenger rail has exclusively international trains. Andorra, San Marino and Vatican City have no passenger rail at all, while every other country with trains operates at least some domestic services. Microstates like Liechtenstein and Monaco are the only cases where any train that stops domestically is already crossing a border in practice.

British Airways West Base is at Terminal 5, and passenger terminals are off-limits, but public transport is easy. Take the Piccadilly line one stop to Hounslow West, then walk 10 minutes to Hounslow High Street.

The Mall Hounslow and the high street have non-spicy options: Tesco and Sainsbury’s sell ready meals, salads and soups you can heat at work. Pret A Manger and Leon offer sandwiches, pasta and soups without spice.

For sit-down daily food, try The Green Kitchen and The Wok Box for mild options, and the food court at the mall for plain pasta and salads. All are reachable by train and foot and suit a recovery diet.

Migration registration in Russia is mandatory for most foreign visitors and is separate from visa requirements. The rule is not “3 days in one place OR 7 days total”, it is both.

Under Federal Law No. 109-FZ, a foreign citizen must be registered within 7 working days of arrival in Russia. The registration is done by the host — hotel, hostel, flat owner, etc. — via the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the host is legally responsible for submitting the notification of arrival.

Hotels do this automatically on check-in. Your friend in Moscow must submit the notification for you, and you must be registered at each address where you stay, even if only for one night. The 7 working day limit is a maximum, not a threshold that exempts you. Staying less than 7 days total does not exempt you if you stay longer than 7 working days, but you cannot “reset the clock” by moving cities. The 3 working day rule your host mentions is the deadline the host has to submit the notification after you arrive at that address, not a limit on how long you can stay without registering.

On your itinerary you will be in Russia for 8 days total, so you are over the 7 working day limit. You will also be staying at your friend’s flat in Moscow on two separate occasions. Your friend must register you each time you arrive at that address, within 3 working days of arrival at that address. If you do not register, both you and your host can be fined, and you may have problems with border control on exit.

There is no advantage to using a German passport instead of a UK passport for registration itself. Both are third-country passports requiring a visa, and the registration rules apply identically. The only practical difference is visa policy and entry conditions.

In practice: hotels in Murmansk and Teriberka will register you automatically. Your Moscow friend must register you for each stay at his flat, ideally on the day of arrival. Keep copies of the registration slip, migration card, and passport with you at all times.

Generally no. B1 allows business meetings, conferences, and short training that is observational and does not provide hands-on skills for U.S. employment. A two-month company training is usually considered substantive, skills-based training intended to benefit your employer, which USCIS treats as work training requiring a specific work visa like M-1 or H-3.

Even with a valid B1/B2 visa, CBP can deny entry if the purpose appears to be training for future employment. You should get a formal assessment from your employer and consult an immigration attorney before traveling.

List the Schengen visit once. The question is about time spent in the Schengen Area as a whole, not in one member state.

Enter Greece as the country of first entry / visa issuing authority, which matches your stamp. For number of days enter the total duration of that Schengen stay, 15 days, not just the one day in Greece.

The entry and exit stamps show one continuous Schengen stay from Greece to France. The UK form wants the country associated with that stay and the overall length of that stay.

If the system forces a single country, add a note in the additional information section stating entry via Greece, exit via France, and that the 15 days covered Greece, Italy, Switzerland and France under one Schengen visa.

Lufthansa Economy Light allows one personal item only, no carry-on. Personal item max 40x30x10 cm, 8 kg. You previously had carry-on because you were on higher fare. Bringing a second bag will incur fee at check-in. Check Lufthansa website for current rules as rules change frequently and enforcement varies by airport so travel light.

No. Lebanese citizens require a visa for Croatia. A visa issued by another EU member state does not exempt you. Croatia is Schengen since 2023, so only a valid Schengen visa, not just any EU visa, permits entry. Check Croatian embassy for current requirements and Romania/Bulgaria remain non-Schengen and also require separate visas for Lebanese holders.

Yes, it is possible but very tight and risky with only a 3 hour layover on Air India.

Your Bangalore-Delhi leg is domestic and arrives at T3, and your Delhi-Vienna leg is international from the same terminal. You will need to collect your checked bags if they were not through-checked, clear immigration for international departure, go through security and reach the international departure gate. Immigration and security queues at T3 can be long, especially in the morning and evening peaks, and Air India requires you to be at the gate 60-75 minutes before departure.

You cannot meet your parents after you have cleared immigration and security, because the departure lounge is airside and closed to visitors. The only place to meet is in the public departure hall before security check. That means your parents would need to come inside the terminal, hand over the packet in the departure area, and you would then proceed through check-in, immigration and security.

With a 3 hour layover you have very little buffer for delays. If your domestic flight is late, or immigration is slow, you will miss your Vienna flight. For a hand-over it is safer to meet them before you leave Bangalore, or to send the packet via courier.

Fairmont Banff Springs and Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise are both iconic, but they serve very different experiences despite being only about 40-60 minutes apart on the Bow Valley Parkway.

Banff Springs is in town, at the foot of Sulphur Mountain. It’s a sprawling, castle-like resort built in 1888, now huge and very much a social hub. You get a full town feel: multiple restaurants, a spa, golf course, conference facilities, and easy walkability to Banff Avenue shops and gondola. It’s busy in summer, family-friendly, and has that grand, slightly chaotic Fairmont resort energy. Rooms vary widely in quality because the hotel is so large and old.

Chateau Lake Louise sits right on the lakeshore, essentially in the park with no town around it. It’s smaller, quieter, and much more focused on the view. The main draw is waking up to turquoise Lake Louise and the Victoria Glacier from your room or the terrace. Dining is more limited and upscale, and the atmosphere is calmer, more romantic and nature-immersed. Access is via a narrow road, so you are more dependent on the hotel for activities.

In short, choose Banff Springs for convenience, amenities and a classic resort buzz, and Chateau Lake Louise for scenery, quiet and direct lake access. Many visitors do both: Banff as a base, Lake Louise for a day or overnight stay.

Yes, you should mention your visa status and sponsor the trip. Include a copy of your valid Schengen business visa and an employment letter or proof of business travel to show ties and purpose of your visit.

For your wife and children, apply for Schengen short-stay tourist visas at the French consulate with jurisdiction over your residence. Submit a family sponsorship letter, your bank statements, employment proof, marriage and birth certificates, travel insurance, hotel bookings and flight itinerary.

Being a homemaker is fine; your sponsorship covers her. The consulate will assess their applications independently, but your valid visa and sponsorship strengthen the application and show you will travel together and return. Apply together if possible.

No. Brazilian law requires every Brazilian citizen to enter and leave Brazil using a valid Brazilian passport. Dual nationality does not exempt you from this obligation.

Brazilian Federal Police will not admit you on an expired Brazilian passport. An expired passport is not considered a valid travel document for entry, even if you also hold a valid US passport. You must present a valid Brazilian passport at immigration on arrival, and Brazilian authorities expect you to depart Brazil on the same document.

For the return to the US, you can and should use your US passport to enter the United States, as US citizens must use a US passport for entry to the US. Using different passports for entry and exit is common and allowed for dual nationals.

In practice, travel to Brazil with an expired Brazilian passport will result in denial of boarding by the airline and/or denial of entry by Brazilian immigration. Renew your Brazilian passport before travel. If you are already abroad, you can request an emergency passport at a Brazilian consulate.

Yes, a name mismatch can cause problems. Global Entry requires all travel documents to match exactly, and CBP will compare your Green Card, passport, and the name you enter on the application.

Apply using the name as it appears on your Green Card, even with the erroneous middle name, and list your passport and state ID as supporting documents. You can note the pending USCIS correction in the application comments.

Once approved, you must present the same Green Card at kiosks and to CBP officers. If you later receive a corrected Green Card, update your Global Entry profile immediately with the new document number and name.

Do not try to use TSA Pre/Global Entry with a different name on your boarding pass. Until the name is consistent across all documents, expect delays or secondary inspection when the mismatch is flagged.

Yes, you can enter Schengen via Italy and exit via the Netherlands. The Schengen area has no internal border controls, so you can travel freely between member states once you are inside. Your return flight can be from Amsterdam, Paris, or any other Schengen airport.

The important point is not the exit point but the visa issuing rule. A Schengen visa issued by Italy means Italy should be your main destination, or at least the first point of entry if stays are balanced. If you will spend more days in the Netherlands than in Italy, or if Italy is not the main purpose of your trip, the visa should have been issued by the Netherlands. Immigration officers in Rome may question this on a first visit.

For your first entry in Rome carry your passport with the valid Schengen visa, a confirmed return or onward ticket to Dubai, travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000 for the whole Schengen area, proof of accommodation for both Italy and the Netherlands, proof of sufficient funds for your stay, and a brief itinerary explaining your travel plan. Keep printed copies.

Be ready to explain why Italy issued the visa and that you will respect the 7 day validity. If the stay in Italy is shorter than in the Netherlands, you risk refusal of entry or future visa problems.

USRP SDR hardware is generally allowed in carry-on. It contains no prohibited items and is not a weapon. Power it off and pack it with your laptop. Security may ask about it; be ready to demonstrate it is a development board. No RF transmission is permitted onboard. Check airline and destination rules for radio equipment in advance.

Yes, several options are within 30-60 min by train from Prague.

Křivoklát area is reachable via Rakovník ~1h, but closer is Vltava valley: reach Černošice or Davle by train 30 min, then easy riverside walks with snow views.

Best for mountains: Brdy Highlands. Take train to Dobříš 50 min then bus to Jince. Forested trails around Skalka and Velká Leč with views, usually snow-covered in December.

Alternatively, Český Kras near Beroun 40 min by train offers limestone plateaus and caves, easy paths with winter scenery.

Dress warmly and check trail conditions before you go.

Visa officers cannot routinely query another country’s immigration database to verify your entries and exits. Immigration systems are sovereign and are not generally shared in real time for visa adjudication purposes.

What officers actually do is rely on passport stamps, your declarations, and corroborating evidence. If a country is stampless, for example many Schengen entries via e-gates, Singapore, UAE transit, or some US land crossings, there will be no visible proof in your passport.

In practice they assess travel history from the itinerary you declare, supporting documents such as boarding passes, hotel receipts, and stamps from neighboring countries that bracket the visit. The consistency of your overall story matters more than a single missing stamp.

Some limited data sharing does exist. Schengen countries share entry/exit data internally, and the US shares entry data with Five Eyes partners under bilateral agreements. Outside those arrangements, direct access is rare.

If you lack stamps, provide secondary evidence where possible, like airline tickets, boarding passes, immigration entry cards, or digital travel records from the airline or border authority. Be honest about gaps. A missing stamp for a known stampless country is normal and will not automatically harm your application if the rest of your history is coherent and verifiable.

No, an invitation letter is not generally required for a Schengen tourist visa. You can apply for a holiday visit without one, provided you submit the standard supporting documents.

Consulates require proof of travel purpose, accommodation, financial means, travel insurance, and return ticket. A hotel booking, itinerary, and bank statements are sufficient for tourism. Invitations are only mandatory for family/friend visits, official trips, or some national visas where the host must sponsor you.

Apply for the country where you will spend the most nights, or first entry. State purpose as tourism. Be consistent with your application and supporting evidence. Some embassies may request invitation for longer stays or if accommodation proof is weak, so check specific consulate requirements.

Scandinavian Mountains Airport is 3.5 hours drive from Trysil. No public bus exists. Options are taxi ~NOK 2500-3000 each way, pre-booked shuttle services, or rental car. Check Trysil Taxi and local transfer companies. Winter road conditions require winter tires. Book ahead in ski season for better availability

Daytime trains exist because not everyone wants to lose a night of sleep or arrive disoriented. A 16:00-23:40 service lets you work, meet people, and be home for dinner before sleeping in your own bed. Overnight trains save a hotel night but cost you rest and flexibility; daytime trains preserve a day.

They also serve travelers who need to arrive fresh for morning meetings, families with children, and passengers with connections. Daylight travel lets you see the route, work on board, and avoid the price and comfort limits of sleeper berths. For many, wasting daylight on a train is less wasteful than wasting a night.

Diabetes medication is generally allowed for personal use, but how you handle it at the airport depends on the country and the type of medication.

Most countries do not require you to declare insulin, test strips, glucose tablets or a glucose meter when you are transiting through or arriving, provided it is for personal use and you carry a doctor’s letter or prescription. The letter is not always mandatory, but it is strongly recommended. It should be on headed paper, state your partner’s name, the diagnosis, the medication name, dosage and that it is for personal use. Keep the medication in its original pharmacy packaging with the label intact.

Some countries do have specific import rules for prescription medicines. For example, the UK allows up to three months’ supply of insulin for personal use without a licence, while the UAE, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and some other states require advance permission or a translated prescription for certain drugs. Needles and lancets are usually permitted in carry-on with a letter, but some airlines and security agencies ask you to declare sharps and show them separately.

Never put insulin in checked baggage; carry it in hand luggage with an ice pack if needed. Carry a copy of the prescription and a note in English, and ideally a translation for the destination country.

Do not use the “nothing to declare” channel if you are unsure about the destination’s rules or are carrying a large supply. If in doubt, declare it. Customs officers are used to this and a brief explanation with documentation is much faster than a dispute at the border.

Check the destination country’s embassy or health travel advice before you travel.

Buying via Opodo/Gotogate is safe; they are licensed agencies. The risk is the 50-minute terminal change at CDG, which is tight. Air France will operate the flights, but Opodo's 'covered' claim is weak if the first flight is delayed and you miss the second. You have no protection from AF for a self-transfer on separate tickets, even if sold. Consider a longer connection.

VLS-TS holders are considered residents and are generally exempt from France’s COVID-19 entry bans. You should be allowed entry as a long-stay visa holder, especially since you have previously lived in France for two years.

Carry your valid VLS-TS, passport, proof of residence, attestation d’hébergement, and your prior residence evidence. Also bring your dog’s health certificate, EU pet passport, and proof of emotional support need.

Check your airline’s policy and the French consulate website for the latest rules before travel, as requirements can change quickly. Keep printed attestations and contact details handy at the border.

This is a known data mismatch problem with the US Arrival/Departure system, not an accusation of wrongdoing on your part.

Your legal stay is recorded by CBP on the I-94, not by a passport stamp. Since 2013 US land and air arrivals for visa waiver and visa holders are recorded electronically and the departure is supposed to be matched automatically from airlineAPIS data. If the airline did not transmit your departure record, or transmitted it under a different name spelling/DOB/passport number, CBP will show you as still in the US.

Do not ignore the notice. Contact the CBP Deferred Inspection office at the port where you arrived and request an I-94 review. You can do this via the CBP Info Center, by email, or in person if you are near a port. Provide your full name, passport number, dates of travel, flight number, and any evidence you have of departure, even indirect.

Evidence helps even if it is not perfect. A police report confirming you were not in the US, family members’ I-94s showing they departed on the same flight, bank/credit card transactions from home country after the departure date, phone roaming records, and the airline booking confirmation showing you were ticketed on that flight are all useful. The airline cannot give passenger lists to you, but CBP can request it under 8 CFR 103.5.

Once the departure is corrected, ask for written confirmation that your record is updated and that no overstay was accrued. Keep that confirmation for future entries.

If you cannot resolve it remotely, you can also file a FOIA request for your CBP travel records to see what they have. For future trips, always save your boarding pass and take a screenshot of your electronic I-94 immediately after arrival at i94.cbp.dhs.gov.

Transit through Frankfurt Airport remains airside and does not constitute entry into Schengen. However the US Presidential Proclamation counts any presence in Schengen within 14 days as disqualifying, even for airport transit. You will be denied boarding unless exempt. Check airline and US embassy guidance before travel for non-US citizens. Transit area is physically inside Schengen territory despite legal distinction.

As a Canadian citizen you can always re-enter Canada. US overstay won't bar return home. At US exit you may face questions, but no penalty. Re-entering US later is problematic: overstay over 1 year triggers 10-year inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(9)(B). Expect secondary inspection and likely denial. Consult an immigration lawyer before travel. Do not lie to officers; honesty is required. You will keep Canadian entry stamp normally.

Request written confirmation of the cancellation reason and reference EC261. Airlines must provide a statement; you can ask for the delay report and maintenance log via data subject access request. Gather boarding passes, tickets, hotel receipts, and screenshots of differing explanations. File a formal compensation claim first; most airlines reject initially. If rejected, use national enforcement body or small claims court. Fraud is hard to prove and costly; focus on EC261 rights. A lawyer is usually unnecessary at this stage now

Denied boarding can occur for: no valid passport/visa, no ticket/seat, no ID, overbooking, missed check-in, health/security risk, disruptive behavior, incorrect name, unpaid fare, expired documents, no boarding pass, weight/balance. See ICAO and IATA guidance. https://www.iata.org/en/iata-recommendations/ Check airline conditions of carriage and government entry requirements before travel for certainty today

No, overnight stays are not allowed in Old Town San Diego State Historic Park. The park is a state historic park and museum complex, not a campground, and it is closed to the public at night.

The park officially closes at sunset, generally around 6 to 7pm depending on the season, and the entrances are locked after hours. Park rangers patrol the grounds and overnight loitering, sleeping, camping or otherwise remaining in the park is prohibited under California State Parks regulations.

There are no designated camping areas, shelters or facilities for overnight visitors inside the historic park boundaries. The historic district is a commercial and residential neighborhood with restaurants, shops and hotels immediately adjacent to the park, which is where visitors should stay.

You can enjoy Old Town during daytime hours and take evening tours and dining in the surrounding area, but you cannot remain in the park itself after closing hours.

You are in a classic power trap, not a normal performance issue. Engaging in a 'master plan' to uncover her will only escalate risk and damage your credibility as Head of HR.

Do not consult the CEO informally. If you do, document facts only in writing and avoid emotional confrontation. A private meeting where you are the messenger for rumors about him will put you in the middle of a retaliation dynamic.

Focus on what you can control: process and documentation. Stop reacting to gossip. Treat all information she shares as unverified. Redirect conversations to work topics and keep a professional boundary. If she approaches you, keep it brief and neutral.

For the rumors about you, do not defend yourself socially. Correct misinformation once, calmly and factually to the people it affects most, then let it go.

Build a paper trail of her behavior that impacts work: missed deliverables, policy violations, hostile interactions. Keep it objective and tied to business impact, not personality. This protects you and gives future managers evidence that is defensible.

If the environment remains unsafe, start planning an exit. Staying to 'not let her win' will cost you more than leaving.

Your handbook sets notice: one day for one-day holiday. Follow it in writing. Cover responsibility usually sits with management, not you. Document incidents, keep union involved, request written procedure from HR. If bullying continues, raise formal grievance with evidence. Prioritise health; seek support.

Target finance-adjacent data roles and frame PhD teaching/RA as experience. Build a portfolio with Kaggle projects, GitHub repos, and a blog on time-series models applied to markets. Network via LinkedIn and alumni. £40k is realistic for junior data scientist roles outside London with a PhD in the UK

Yes, you are entitled to ask your boss for clarity, but approach it as seeking information, not as a confrontation.

You are working with second-hand rumors. That is incomplete and often inaccurate information, and acting on it can create unnecessary anxiety and damage trust. Your boss is in the best position to give you the most accurate picture of where things stand.

Ask for a private, low-pressure check-in. Frame it around your commitment, not the rumor. For example: "I’ve heard some informal talk about staffing needs on other teams and want to make sure I’m aligned with your priorities for my role. Is there anything I should be aware of regarding my current assignment?"

This opens the door without accusing anyone of secrecy. If a transfer is being discussed, you will get a more honest answer than from hallway whispers. If it is not, you stop worrying.

Do not lead with an ultimatum about resigning. Telling your boss you will quit if moved will be seen as a threat and will likely reduce his willingness to fight for you. If a move is proposed, you can then discuss your career goals, interests, and why you are a better fit for your current team, and only later raise a resignation if you truly have no flexibility.

Focus on clarity first, options second.

This is a health and safety issue, not just an annoyance. Sustained exposure to loud noise, especially when you are compensating by maxing out your headphones, can cause hearing damage and headaches. You need to address it before it affects you.

Start with low friction options. Try a white noise machine or a small fan near your cube to add masking sound without increasing headphone volume. Noise-canceling headphones, particularly over-ear ANC models, will perform much better than standard Bluetooth earbuds for constant speech.

If that doesn't help, document the problem objectively. Note dates, times, duration, and what you were doing when it was disruptive. Record a short phone audio sample from your desk, not to shame anyone but to show the decibel level to management.

Then raise it professionally. Talk to your own team lead first, framing it as impact on your work and health: "I’m getting 4-5 hours of very loud conversation from the neighboring team that I can hear even with headphones at max volume, and it’s giving me headaches." Ask if they can speak with the other team’s manager about keeping voices down in shared space.

If nothing changes, escalate to HR or facilities with your log. Request accommodations like a desk move away from the hallway, a partial panel, or a quiet zone policy. You deserve to work without risking your hearing.

Don't share details. Say you parted due to miscommunication and learned about professional boundaries. Own your part, show growth, and focus on strengths. Employers hire for future performance, not past drama. Keep it brief, positive, and forward-looking and ready to contribute immediately

It's understandable to feel frustrated, but with only a couple months tenure it's risky to frame this as "he makes $5k more than me." Managers will hear that as a complaint, not a conversation, and it can label you as difficult early on.

Instead, focus on your own value and future trajectory. Wait until you have a performance check-in, ideally 3-6 months in, and come prepared with data about your contributions, not his salary. Document what you've delivered, learned, and taken ownership of since starting.

Then ask about compensation philosophy, not parity. Try: "I'm really enjoying the work here and want to make sure I'm growing in the right way. Could you help me understand how base salary and raises are determined here, and what milestones I should hit to be considered for a market adjustment?" This invites transparency without accusing anyone of unfairness.

If you do want to address the disparity directly, you need evidence, not anecdote. One data point about a peer isn't enough and can be explained by negotiation, prior experience, location, signing bonus conversion, etc. Use market data from levels.fyi, Glassdoor, and your recruiter to understand the band for your title.

If after that conversation you get vague answers, you can ask for a formal compensation review in 6-12 months with clear goals. If the gap persists and you have documented strong performance, that's the time to negotiate, not now. Protect your reputation first; you can always address pay later with a stronger case.

If you discover systemic bias, consider speaking to HR confidentially about the pay band rather than naming the colleague.

Wait a day or two, then gently bump the thread. Acknowledge their busy schedule and reference the original question.

Example: “Hi [Name], hope your week is going well. I know things are busy, so I just wanted to gently bump my question from Tuesday about X. No rush at all, just let me know when you have a moment. Thanks so much!”

This is polite, non-accusatory, and gives them an easy out.

I've seen people move from corporate finance to family businesses. Skills like discipline, analysis and stakeholder management transfer well. Start part-time or unpaid trial while keeping HSBC income if possible. Test fit, clarify roles, and set boundaries early to avoid family friction. Crisis can be catalyst, but don't burn bridges before making decision

Job hopping is a signal, not a verdict. HR will notice the pattern, but what matters is the story you tell about it and how you frame each move.

You are 22-23 now with five roles in three years. That is fast, but you also have a coherent narrative: you were learning, you left for ethics, and you are now stabilizing. That is defensible if you own it.

First, stop treating the second role as a failure. You were promoted beyond your skill level, performed well for six months, then a personal crisis impacted performance despite management support. That shows self-awareness, not flakiness. Frame it as a stretch role you took on early, learned from, and left when you recognized the mismatch. Do not hide it.

Second, the first, third and fourth exits are actually positives for most international employers. Leaving a company that cooked books and paid envelope salaries, leaving due to mismanagement that killed a startup, and leaving over unfair competition are all principled exits. They signal integrity and judgment. Name them clearly: ethical concerns, toxic management, unsustainable business practices.

Third, your current role is your anchor. A year and counting, with intent to stay longer, helps a lot. It shows you can settle when the environment is right. Use it as your reference point.

In interviews, keep it brief and forward-looking. One sentence per role: what you did, what you learned, why you left. No long apologies. Then pivot to what you want next and why this company fits.

On a CV, group early contract or junior roles if relevant, use a functional summary for the first two years, and make sure dates line up. Be ready for reference checks.

International employers care less about perfect tenure and more about consistency, growth, and risk. You have a pattern of leaving bad situations early rather than staying and becoming disengaged. That is a feature, not a bug, if you present it calmly.

Your history will raise questions. A clear, honest narrative will answer them.

Contact the new employer immediately in writing and ask for a firm written start date and confirmation the offer remains valid. Do not assume goodwill. Ask if they can provide an advance or a retainer to cover your gap. Simultaneously, talk to your current manager about pausing or withdrawing your notice, explaining the situation has changed beyond your control. If your company has no grace period, request to stay on unpaid leave or extend notice if possible. Start actively job searching now as a backup. In India, verbal assurances are weak; get everything in writing before making further commitments and protect your financial security now.

No. You negotiated in good faith and the company agreed. Delaying now creates precedent and signals mistrust. If you're worried, offer flexibility on bonuses or hours, not a pay cut you need. Staying loyal long-term matters more than one gesture in a crisis.

I'm not a lawyer, and Chilean labor law is complex, so please consult a local labor attorney or union representative.

Chile is under a state of catastrophe, but that does not automatically grant individual right to refuse work. Under Chilean Labor Code, you can only refuse work for justified reasons like imminent danger to life or health. COVID-19 risk may qualify, but you would need to prove it is specific and imminent, not general fear.

ILO conventions on occupational safety and health require employers to provide safe workplaces, but enforcement is national. You could formally request remote work citing family vulnerability and wife's medical condition, requesting reasonable accommodation.

Document your request in writing, cite your wife's diagnosis and children's home care needs, and ask for risk assessment. If refused, you could file a complaint with Dirección del Trabajo.

Do not unilaterally stop commuting without written agreement, as that can be considered unjustified absence. Seek medical certificate and legal advice first.

Roughly add 25–35% on top of your current salary. Employers pay ~15% social insurance plus withholding costs; as 業務委託 you pay both halves of pension/health, national tax, and lose employment insurance. For 600万円–1億円, target 750–1.35億円 to keep net take-home similar, plus buffer for unpaid leave, equipment and risk and business expenses and uncertainty

Create low-pressure spaces, not obligations. Add a #watercooler channel for non-work chat, and a weekly optional virtual coffee with random pairings. Keep cameras on for 5 min pre-meeting mingling and share personal updates in stand-ups. Model vulnerability first. Spontaneity grows when people feel safe, not scheduled.

Getting from 0 to 1 means creating something from nothing, not just improving existing. 0 to 1 is invention, 1 to n is scaling.

In software management context, it means building a new team, product, or capability from scratch: hiring, defining vision, setting process, delivering first working version.

Not just "get team up and running", it's about proving you can create initial value where none existed, then iterate. Interviewers want examples of founding, not just optimizing.

Show how you identified problem, assembled people, made first decisions, shipped MVP and learned. That's the 0 to 1 story they want. If you only scaled existing teams, you did 1 to n, not 0 to 1.

You can refuse this professionally without it sounding suspicious by framing it around privacy and personal safety, not secrecy.

Start by thanking them for including you and then state a clear boundary. Something like: "Thanks for thinking of me. For personal privacy reasons I would prefer not to have my photo and name published on the public website. I’m happy to be listed with just my name and title if needed, but I’d like to opt out of the photo and public profile."

Companies are used to privacy requests. In Europe you have strong backing for this. Under GDPR, personal data including photos and employment details published publicly must have a lawful basis and your consent. You can explicitly withdraw consent for public processing of your image and personal data. You don’t need to give a detailed explanation, just a preference.

If they push that it’s “standard”, keep it brief and consistent: "I understand it’s standard practice, but this is a personal preference I’d like to respect. I’m comfortable being in the internal directory, just not the public one."

If you want to reduce Google exposure, you can also ask for a practical compromise: no photo, no detailed bio, and no link to a dedicated profile page. Just a name and role in a plain list is much harder to surface in search results than a page with your photo and a heading with your name.

If you want to go further after they publish, you can use Google’s removal tools for personal information and request the company to remove or de-index your profile. You can also ask the company to add a robots.txt or noindex tag to employee pages, which many firms do for privacy reasons.

You don’t look like you have something to hide by wanting basic online privacy. Many people, especially those with unusual or easily searchable names, choose to limit their digital footprint. A calm, polite, and consistent request is usually respected, and it’s easier for HR to process than a debate about why.

Keep the tone cooperative, not confrontational, and put it in writing so you have a record.

Relax, these are minor discrepancies, not deception. You proactively disclosed both the correct percentage and the contact-center gap to BGV, which shows integrity. Most companies care about honesty and current skills, not perfect resumes. Focus on your performance, not past anxiety. The conditional offer is a strong sign they want you.

That clause is not normal and is unusually broad. Standard employment IP clauses cover work created during employment, or using company resources, not pre-existing IP you created before you started.

Signing away all prior IP, with only an opt-out list, puts the burden on you to remember and disclose everything, and creates risk the company could claim ownership of personal projects, open-source contributions, writing, code, patents, etc.

In some jurisdictions such sweeping assignments are unenforceable, especially for IP created before employment, but you shouldn't rely on that. It's also a red flag about how the company handles IP.

Normal practice is a carve-out: you list pre-existing IP you want to keep, and the company agrees not to claim it, while assigning only IP created in scope of employment.

Ask to narrow the clause to post-employment work only, or to a specific carve-out list of your existing IP. Have a lawyer review local enforceability before signing.

Yes, it can be acceptable, but timing and framing matter a lot. Asking for feedback is professional if you do it to improve the process, not to re-litigate the hire.

Wait a few weeks until the new hire is settled and feels safe. Make the request opt-in and low pressure, and be clear it will not affect their role. Frame it as process improvement.

For example: “I’m working on improving our interview process. Since you’ve just gone through it, I’d value your candid perspective on what felt clear, what was confusing, or what felt unfair.”

Keep questions about experience, not performance. Ask about communication, clarity of expectations, the technical assessment realism, pacing, and how respected they felt. Avoid asking why they were chosen or about specific answers.

For your concern about the technical assessment, one person’s view is limited. Gather anonymized feedback from multiple recent candidates, successful and not, and present themes to HR. That gives you data to argue that marking a methodological but incomplete solution the same as no attempt is counterproductive.

Offer a short written form or a 10 minute chat, thank them regardless, and do not make it feel like an evaluation of them.

First, separate the two issues. Your employer owes you market rate for the work you do, not a penalty for income you earn outside work. If your boss is explicitly using your side hustle as a reason to withhold raises, document what was said, when and how.

Build a performance case, not an emotional one. For seven years you’ve taken on more responsibility with only COLA raises while newer coworkers earn more. List specific contributions, projects led, revenue impact, and skills gained. Benchmark external salary ranges for your role in your city and industry.

Present it as a retention conversation. Reassure that your side work does not interfere with hours, performance, confidentiality, or company interests, and is done on your own time. If there is a real conflict, be prepared to discuss boundaries.

Ask for clear criteria: what measurable milestones would trigger a raise and on what timeline. Get the response in writing.

In parallel, reduce your dependency. Diversify customer acquisition so you are not trapped by this job. If the company continues to underpay despite documented value, start interviewing elsewhere now, even if you stay for now.

When your recruiter forwarded the thread, what recipients see depends on how it was forwarded. If he used Forward, the email client typically includes the original message as an attachment or quoted text, but only the addresses you put in To/CC on your reply receive it. People who were removed from the chain are not automatically added back. Your reply only goes to the prospective employer and your recruiter, since you copied him. Past recipients cannot see your correspondence unless they are explicitly included or the recruiter used a method that exposes the address list.

Focus on understanding the team rhythm, not just hours. Ask about how they structure their day and collaborate with colleagues in different time zones.

Try: 'How does the team typically organize its day? Are there core hours for meetings or collaboration, and is flexibility common for focused work?' or 'What does a typical week look like here in terms of pace and deadlines?'

This shows you care about integration and performance, not minimizing effort. It also gives you real insight into expectations and presenteeism culture without sounding lazy at all.

Start professionally but warmly. Thank him for the intro, mention your mutual connection by name, and keep tone friendly. Attach resume and brief cover note tailored to the startup. Reference his 'F*** yeah' energy lightly if comfortable, but don't mimic profanity. Ask for a 15-minute chat about roles for new grads. Close politely, and let him set the formality level going forward. You can follow his lead on tone in replies. Good luck!

You can't control a competitive culture, but you can control where you place yourself and how you respond.

First, recognize the signal. When teams feel threatened by someone improving processes, it's often about status loss, not you. The developers weren't fighting your ideas, they were fighting the loss of ownership. Name that explicitly early: "I'm here to support the work you already own, not replace it." Invite them to co-author changes.

Second, stop winning technical arguments. Long explanations prove you're right and make people feel smaller. Instead ask: "What concern is behind that?" Translate their resistance into requirements and give them credit publicly when their input improves the solution.

Third, choose environments that reward collaboration. In interviews, ask how teams handle disagreement, how promotions are decided, and whether post-mortems are blameless. Look for shared OKRs, rotation of lead roles, and leaders who praise collective outcomes.

Fourth, protect your energy. You can't convert a battlefield into a team overnight. If a client consistently undermines you, treat it as data about fit and move on. Your experience is valuable where psychological safety exists.

Finally, consider shifting your role. Coaching, internal enablement, or smaller teams often attract people who want to build together rather than compete.

You didn't fail the industry; you outgrew the parts that reward politics over craft.

This is a good problem to have, and it’s understandable you don’t want to make it awkward.

First, consider why he might be under-reporting. It could be modesty or insecurity about his speed, a misunderstanding of what counts as billable time, a desire to appear efficient, or even a belief that you’ll think less of him if he logs more hours. With a young, fast-learning freelancer, it’s often a mix of not wanting to feel like a burden and not being sure what you actually want tracked.

Don’t frame it as an accusation. Approach it as a process check-in, not a performance review. Pick a neutral moment and ask about his workflow: “I’ve noticed your timesheets are consistently low compared to the scope of work you’re delivering. I want to make sure we’re capturing the work accurately so you’re paid fairly and we have good records for planning.”

That signals you’re on his side. You can add that you value his talent and want him to feel comfortable logging all time, including learning, research, and revisions, if that’s how you bill. If he’s hourly, make clear you want accurate hours, not fewer hours.

If he still under-reports, you can set a simple expectation: “Please log time as you work, and if you’re unsure what to include, ask me.” Keep it brief and document the conversation.

You’re paying above market and have a meritocratic culture, so reinforce that. The goal is to protect him from underpaying himself and protect you from scope creep surprises later.

Project X is a retention problem, not just a technical one. No team wants to own it because the risk is high and the reward is invisible.

Stop trying to “turn it around” with motivation. Get clarity and protection first.

Ask leadership for a written decision: Is Project X a strategic must-finish or a legacy to be retired? Mixed signals are why people leave it. If it is to finish, get a formal charter with a defined scope, success criteria, and end date. If it is to be shelved, get that in writing too.

If you must stay involved, negotiate boundaries. Request a small, time-boxed team with rotation so no one is stuck long term, and make the extreme customer requirements explicit in a requirements review with product and the customer. Document what is impossible with current technology now, not after months of work.

Make the cost visible. Track attrition, rework, and opportunity cost and present it monthly. People avoid the project because it feels like a career dead end. Give people a clear exit ramp and credit for containment, not heroics.

If leadership won’t commit, the professional move is to decline ownership and protect your own work.

The void on LinkedIn is real in quantum computing, and it’s not just you. The field is still tiny, hiring is concentrated, and most roles are filled by referral or through research networks before they ever hit public boards.

Your background is actually a strong fit, but you are competing in a market that values depth in a very specific stack. Post-quantum cryptography experience plus hands-on algorithm coding is valuable, especially for security, software, and applications teams. Frame it that way rather than as general physics interest.

First, narrow your target. The industry is not monolithic. There are hardware companies like IBM, Rigetti, IonQ, PsiQuantum, academic labs, national labs, and software/algorithms firms like Q-CTRL, Zapata, and Xanadu. Security-focused quantum roles are growing faster than pure hardware roles right now. Look at post-quantum cryptography teams at Cloudflare, NIST, ISARA, PQShield. That is a more realistic on-ramp.

Second, make your work visible. Recruiters in quantum rarely search LinkedIn keywords, they search GitHub, arXiv, and community talks. Put your proof-of-concept demos on GitHub with clear READMEs, notebooks showing Qiskit, Cirq or Q# runs, and write short blog posts explaining the vulnerability you found and how you mitigated it. That becomes your portfolio.

Third, use community, not job boards. Join Quantum Open Source Foundation, Qiskit Advocate program, and the Qiskit Slack. Attend Qiskit Global Summer School, Q2B, Qubit by Qubit. Quantum Computing Stack Exchange and the r/QuantumComputing Discord are where people post unlisted internships. Hackathons do exist and help: Qiskit Global Summer School Hackathon, IBM Quantum Hackathon, QHack by Xanadu, and the annual Quantum Computing Hackathon at Q2B. They are good for networking, not direct hiring.

Finally, get a champion. Find 2-3 people working where you want to work, read their papers, and send a concise, specific note referencing their work and your relevant demo. Ask for a 15 minute chat, not a job. That referral converts at a much higher rate than cold applications.

You are in the right field, you just need to be visible where hiring actually happens.

No, a drug test does not automatically mean a background check will follow. Companies choose screening types separately based on role and policy. They may add a background check later, but you should only expect what was explicitly communicated to you today.

Six months in a new domain at a big company is a normal ramp-up period, especially when you moved from .NET industrial automation to C++ performance modeling of hardware. Feeling exhausted and worried about your progress doesn’t mean you are failing, it means you are learning a complex stack under remote conditions.

First, separate learning debt from performance debt. You were hired one level above entry because of your degree and experience, not because you already knew this HW block. The first 6-12 months in semiconductor modeling is largely about building a mental map: acronyms, datapaths, verification flows, how the model maps to silicon. Running hardware tests, doing research, and getting oriented to the codebase is real work, not procrastination. That superficial knowledge you describe — knowing where to find information — is actually a critical early milestone. Experts know what they don’t know and where to look.

The lead’s questions are a good sign, not a warning. Asking how you feel, how the team can improve, and advising you to talk to senior engineers is coaching, not criticism. Leads often check in at the 6-month mark to calibrate support. If he were truly unhappy, the conversation would be more specific about deliverables and timelines.

To reduce burnout and anxiety, make your learning visible and bounded.

Create a weekly learning log. Pick 3-5 concepts from the hardware domain you encountered that week and write a one-paragraph explanation in your own words. Link them to your model work. This turns vague “I don’t know enough” into concrete progress you can show.

Time-box learning. Allocate 60-90 minutes a day for deep domain study and protect the rest for deliverable work. When you are debugging, you are not supposed to also be learning the whole architecture from scratch in the same hour. Switch modes deliberately.

Use the lead’s advice strategically. Don’t just “talk to senior engineers.” Go in with specific questions: “When I ran test X, the counter Y behaved like Z. Is that expected for this block under condition A?” That shows you are engaging with the system, not asking for a lecture, and it builds relationships.

Manage remote isolation. Working from home removes osmotic learning. Schedule 2-3 short, recurring 15 minute syncs with a buddy or senior engineer, not ad-hoc. Ask for a 30 minute walkthrough of one subsystem with a diagram you can annotate.

Finally, reframe the fear. The fear of performing inadequately is often a sign you care about quality. In HW modeling, a slow correct model beats a fast wrong model. Your lead helped you zero in on a bug, which means you are already contributing to the debugging loop.

If exhaustion persists for more than a couple weeks, check basics: sleep, movement, boundaries between work and home, and whether you have one trusted person on the team you can be honest with. Six months is early. Keep documenting what you learn, keep asking targeted questions, and let your lead see the trajectory, not just the current depth.
